> Thus, in most studies, LGBTQ+ participants were compared with non-LGBTQ+ samples.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Queering the Pages: A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals [Preregistration]
table.type_of_review: A systematic literature review of published articles, including but not limited to original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials, and corrections of previously published articles.
table.review_stages:
•	October 2023: Preparation of Preregistration
•	November 2023: Preregistration
•	December 2023: Preregistration and Literature Search
•	January 2024: Screening
•	February 2024: Data Extraction
•	March 2024: Critical Appraisal 
•	May and June 2024: Narrative Synthesis
These steps are described in further detail below.
table.current_review_stage: Preregistration and preparation of literature search
table.description:
Interest and subsequent research in the field of LGBTQ+ psychology, that is lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and other non-heterosexual and non-cisgender identities, has increased significantly in recent decades (Walch et al., 2020). In light of this surge, many researchers, publishers, and institutions aim to integrate an LGBTQ+ inclusive approach into their fields of study. Especially in the field of educational psychology, creating an inclusive and safe environment for students at school, is regarded as a necessity for positive student outcomes (Cerezo & Bergfeld, 2013; Fields & Wotipka, 2020). Calls have been made to the field of educational psychology, to increase inclusivity of diverse perspectives relating to sexual orientation and gender identity. As already stated in one such call made by Espelage (2016) in the Journal of School Psychology, a lot of work is yet to be done. 
Indeed, several existing articles in educational psychology journals explore the impact that identifying outside of heterosexual and cisgender norms can have on youth (Abreu et al., 2021; Day et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2020). They illustrate that the process and outcome of a student coming to terms with their LGBTQ+ identity is often mitigated by their school environment, be it peers, teachers, counsellors, or curricula (Abreu et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022). Thus, several factors relating to school experience have been established to determine the well-being of LGBTQ+ students both in their time at school and in later life (Kosciw et al., 2012; Kosciw et al., 2014). Taken together, LGBTQ+ issues in educational psychology are worth investigating to provide instruction on how to create safe environments for both LGBTQ+ students as well as educators, as this is crucial to well-being.
However, this area of research is somewhat underdeveloped in the field of educational
psychology and existing literature in the most cited journals from this field remains sparse. Literature on LGBTQ+ issues is mainly published in LGBTQ+ psychology journals, which in turn emphasize the importance of the inclusion of such topics in educational (or school) psychology (Heck et al., 2016; Snapp et al., 2015). Existing research in educational psychology oftentimes focuses solely on negative themes, such as exclusion, bullying, or discrimination, and their damaging impact on LGBTQ+ students (Birkett et al., 2009; Heck et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2011). 
Large gaps in studies published in educational psychology journals are evident. As such, research on the positive effect of equity and inclusion of LGBTQ+ students in an everyday school environment is less frequent. Thus, the evidence base is scattered, and a comprehensive overview of LGBTQ+ research is needed. Considering this need, a systematic literature review could bring clarity and order into the field. Further, such a systematic review would contribute by reliably illustrating what has already been researched and achieved. At the same time, a systematic review could indicate what is still missing and needs to be explored further, in order to claim that educational psychology is indeed inclusive of LGBTQ+ issues. As such, a scientometric approach will be utilized by the authors of this study. The field of scientometrics concerns itself with measuring and analyzing scholarly literature, including a measurement of the impact of research papers and academic journals (Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012). 
This systematic literature review aims to critically examine the current stance of research on LGBTQ+ issues in schools, in the field of educational psychology. To address the research questions below, we will conduct a systematic review of eligible articles found in 31 of the most cited journals from the field of educational psychology, as illustrated in our search strategy below. To this end, an already existing literature review conducted on this topic by Jones et al. (2018) will be updated and significantly expanded. A further search of similar reviews has revealed two prior articles on LGTBQ+ issues in educational and school psychology (Abreu et al. 2021; Leung et al. 2022). In our systematic literature review, we will address shortcomings of these three literature reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022).
Abreu et al. (2021) reviewed recent literature from 11 school psychology journals, determined as relevant to assess school experiences of LGBTQ+ individuals. The authors identified different themes, such as: oppressive attitudes and behaviors toward LGBTQ+ students and subsequent negative outcomes, LGBTQ+ specific advocacy and support in schools as well as recommendations, LGBTQ+ victimization, bystanders and perpetrators, inclusion policies, and faculty training. The authors maintained an intersectional perspective and focused largely on prevention and intervention practices to create a safe environment in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors reviewed literature published in the field of school psychology only, in order to assess how empirical studies have portrayed the experiences of LGBTQ+ students in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors also chose this approach based on the importance of LGBTQ+ research in the field of school psychology, in laying the groundwork to create affirming spaces for LGBTQ+ students at school. 
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) conducted a systematic search across the disciplines of education and psychology (for more details, see below). They explored existing social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth in schools, using Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992) as an organizational framework. Identified social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate (Leung et al., 2022). The authors illustrated current research on outcomes for LGBTQ+ youth and various barriers to support LGBTQ+ youth in schools (Leung et al., 2022). They also examined how to adapt existing support systems to promote positive outcomes, as well as areas for future research on LGBTQ+ youth (Leung et al., 2022).
In our systematic literature review, we aim to identify current areas of research on LGBTQ+ issues, illustrate where research is missing, state themes future research can expand upon, and highlight how educators can use this information to expand support systems for LGBTQ+ individuals at schools. We will refer to several methods and themes from all three reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022) when conducting the current systematic review. 
The systematic literature review conducted by Abreu et al. (2021) focused on counseling related themes and literature, reviewing empirical studies from the field of school psychology. Moreover, the systematic review conducted by Jones at al. (2018) reviewed all published literature on LGBTQ+ youth in schools from the field of educational psychology, which we will do similarly. However, in comparison to Jones et al. (2018), this systematic review will also broaden the focus beyond LGBTQ+ students and will include LGBTQ+ staff where possible, similarly to the scoping review written by Leung et al. (2022). 
We will take search terms used by Abreu et al. (2021), Jones et al. (2018), and Leung et al. (2022) into account when conducting the literature search. Jones et al. (2018) included research that focused solely on sexual identity minorities. As such, gender minorities are often excluded in research in various fields of psychology, in favor of research on LGB identities (Treadway & Yoakam, 1992; Meyer, 2003; Plöderl & Tremblay, 2015). By including both gender and sexual identity minorities, we will build upon the systematic review by Jones et al. (2018). This entails using many search terms to capture a large variety of identities that are included under the LGBTQ+ umbrella (see Query String below). Methodologically, we will also advance upon the review of Jones et al. (2018). We will document search, screening, and extraction procedures in detail, comparable to Abreu at al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022). Additionally, we will preregister this study to meet open science standards and will conduct a systematic review that is comprehensible to any audience, and can be easily replicated as all material and data will be documented and made publicly available. 
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) organized literature identified into various categories of social support for LGBTQ+ students based on Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992). These categories of social support included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate. Depending on our results, we may examine various support systems in a similar framework, however, we have no intention to conduct our review based on these predetermined support categories. Leung et al. (2022) excluded any research that is unrelated to school environments and where social support outcomes where not related to students (i.e., teachers, parents). Consulting a social science librarian, Leung et al. (2022) followed the methodological scoping review approach designed by Arksey and O’Malley (2007), searching across the disciplines of education and psychology. The purpose of their study was to create a less systematic nevertheless broad overview of social support systems, which was met through this strategy (Leung et al, 2022). A scoping review was also chosen to include both empirical and non-empirical literature, the latter meaning books, book chapters, case reports, and reviews. However, a scoping review search strategy utilizes a less defined search. We will conduct a full systematic literature review using precise search terms listed below. Of note, Leung et al. (2022) analyzed which of the many terms of the LGBTQ+ acronym were used most often and which were used least in existing literature, which we aim to repeat once articles are extracted. We would additionally like to adopt the approach of Leung et al. (2022) to provide a positive outlook on LGBTQ+ youth’s school experiences, however broadening this focus beyond youth to staff and care-givers as mentioned above.
Abreu et al. (2021) identified all studies in the field of school psychology published between 2009 and 2019. Leung et al. (2022) extracted articles published between 2007 and 2021. Similarly to Jones et al. (2018), in our systematic review we will include every article published in the most cited journals of educational psychology, including most recent publications. The latter is important to account for rapid changes in LGBTQ+ populations, that can be observed in the current time.

table.research_questions:
We will examine the following three research questions:

Research Question 1: To what extent is LGBTQ+ centered research represented in the field of educational psychology? 

Research Question 2: What are the common themes and trends in LGBTQ+ centered research in the field of educational psychology thus far?

Research Question 3: Where can major gaps in research on LGBTQ+ topics be identified and subsequently, which topics can future research focus on? Expectation 1: We expect that existing research that focuses on LGBTQ+ issues in educational psychology is sparse and issues are only reported by half of the reviewed journals, similarly to Jones et al. (2018). 

Expectation 2: We expect to find that research focuses mainly on negative aspects related to LGBTQ+ identities in educational contexts (e.g., bullying, discrimination, or exclusion).

Expectation 3: To a lesser extent, we expect to find research on the positive effect of teacher and care-giver support, support groups, and measures taken by schools regarding LGBTQ+ issues. 

Expectation 4: We expect to identify several research gaps in articles published in the relevant journals. Such research gaps could potentially include a focus on negative outcomes, issues only relevant to specific age groups, and more student- compared to teacher-focused research. We aim to showcase a range of future research topics deducted from these research gaps.
table.secondary_research_question_s: Research Question 4: How can the common themes and trends identified be applied to guide educators and care-givers of LGBTQ+ students?

table.databases:

(2018), we will use the most cited journals to receive an accurate portrayal of the field of educational psychology. Jones et al. (2018) identified 21 journals. Abreu et al. (2021) examined articles in 11 school psychology journals. We will use 31 journals, all of which have a Journal Impact Factor in the upper two quartiles in the field of educational psychology. Specifically, with a Journal Impact Factor in the two upper quartiles since 2022 as per SCIMAGO https://jcr-clarivate-com.proxy.bnl.lu/jcr/browse-journals (accessed on November 08th 2023). In accordance with criteria set by us (see inclusion and exclusion criteria below) all relevant articles will be extracted, as this specific scientometric approach has been previously established (see also Fong et al., 2022).
We will search relevant articles including, but not limited to original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials, and corrections of previously published articles, published in the 31 most cited journals educational psychology. table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will include articles which fulfill all of the following criteria:
•	Relevant articles include original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials and corrections of previously published articles
•	We will only include articles published in relevant journals (listed above) 
•	Literature and data found refers to an educational context
•	LGBTQ+ issues are a main topic of the article and are not only discussed or mentioned

We will exclude articles if they fulfill one or more of the following exclusion criteria:
•	For phase one of the search: The abstract or keywords reporting the results of the study are not available
•	For phase two of the search: The full text, or secondary sources reporting the results of the study are not available
•	Search terms are only found in author names
Additionally, overlap between otherwise independent studies will be checked and dealt with after the screening.
table.query_strings:
To ensure a comprehensive, yet specific search, we created our search terms focusing on words that relate to LGBTQ+ identities. Concretely, we provide a selection of LGBTQ+ related words adapted from search terms applied in previous reviews on LGBTQ+ topics (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022). Leung et al. (2022) emphasize that the use of search terms can hinder capturing all identities included in the LGBTQ+ community, particularly gender minority identities. Thus, we will include a wide range of search terms for gender minorities as well as sexual identity minorities. The use of several outdated terms was a deliberate choice made by the authors to identify literature that may originate from a period where such terms were used commonly (e.g., hermaphroditism). 

We will search the titles, abstracts, and keywords of the identified 31 journals with the following search term (example search term in ERIC):

(Sexuality OR sexual minorit* OR gender minorit* OR sexual divers* OR gender divers* OR queer OR LGB* OR GLB* OR 2SLGBTQ+ OR sexual orientation* OR sexual identit* OR gender identit* OR same-sex OR hermaphroditism OR transsexual* OR sapphic OR achillean OR homosexual* OR lesbian* OR gay* OR bisexual* OR demigender* OR bigender* OR agender OR demisexual* OR transgender* OR gender express* OR gender expans* OR gender fluid OR transsexual* OR trans masc* OR trans fem* OR non-binary OR N2 gender-queer OR N2 gender-fluid OR N2 gender non-conforming OR intersexual* OR pansexual* OR asexual* OR aromanti* OR N2 coming-out OR heteronormativ* OR cissex* OR heterorsexis* OR non-heterosexual* OR cisnormativit* OR homophobi* OR transphobi*)

Examples of our screening forms can be found online (see QUEER-SR_Screening_Sheet.xlsx in Screener Instructions).

Both Abreu et al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022) included further search terms, accounting for other areas relevant to research questions. Leung et al (2022) searched LGBTQ+ terms (e.g., homosexuality, bisexuality, gender identity), school related terms (e.g., high school students) and social support terms (e.g., peers). Abreu et al. (2021) searched LGBTQ+ terms (i.e., sexual and gender identity, LGBTQ, GLBTQ, LGB, GLB, queer, gay, homosexuality, male homosexuality, bisexuality, lesbian, trans, transgender, sexual orientation, sexual identity, sexual minority, gender identity, gender expression, gender diversity, gender expansive, genderqueer, and gender fluid),  school related terms (i.e., student, students, alumnus, alumni, former student, and k‐12 students), and school psychology terms (i.e., school psychology, school psychologist(s), and psychology in school(s)). We will focus solely on terms related to the LGBTQ+ umbrella, to identify all articles on LGBTQ+ issues published in the field of educational psychology without restriction.
table.search_validation_procedure: We will validate the search results on ERIC by applying the same search terms on official journal websites and comparing results there, such as APA PsycNet (https://psycnet.apa.org/), Sage (https://journals.sagepub.com/), Taylor and Francis (https://www.tandfonline.com/), or other official journal inventories depending on search results. Any other articles found in only one of either database will be included in the search and later screened and coded.

table.search_strategy_justification:
This systematic review is conducted to assess the current stance of published articles in journals of educational psychology. Therefore, a search using a database with published journal articles from the field of education shall be utilized. 
The database ERIC is an internet-based bibliographic and full-text database of education research and information. Founded in 1964, ERIC is designed for user groups such as academics, researchers, educators, policymakers, and the general public (https://eric.ed.gov/?faq). Considering this, ERIC is a suitable database to conduct the present systematic review for the field of educational psychology.
table.miscellaneous_search_strategy_details: No miscellaneous details are to be reported at the present time.
table.screening_stages:
We will screen, extract, and review the selected literature, following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, which is an addition to the methods used by Jones et al. (2018) and was also used by Abreu et al. (2021). We anticipate to identify between 40 and 60 articles within the 31 listed journals. The previous study from Leung et al. (2022) identified 54 articles and that of Abreu et al. (2021) identified 23 articles to extract. No such specifications were made by Jones et al. (2018).
The first author will screen and review the literature, and then discuss results with all authors. Two authors will screen at least 20% of the articles. We will use the deduplication feature implemented in Zotero to screen for duplicates. Other duplicates will be identified manually through the screening and coding processes.
table.screened_fields_blinding: We will locate the search terms listed above in titles, abstracts, and keywords of published articles. The first author will search for and screen the literature independently, we will then have one other author double-screen 20% of the findings, and all results will be included in the systematic review; therefore, no blinding is necessary.
table.used_exclusion_criteria:
We will exclude articles during the screening if they fulfill one or more of the following exclusion criteria:
•	For phase one of the search: The abstract or keywords reporting the results of the study are not available
•	For phase two of the search: The full text, or secondary sources reporting the results of the study are not available
•	Search terms are only found in author names
table.screener_instructions: Following PRISMA guidelines, journal articles will be identified in the relevant journals. In a first phase, using the database ERIC, we will collect articles containing search words in titles, abstracts, or in key word sections. Articles found will be cross-validated with online journal inventories, such as APA PsycNet (https://psycnet.apa.org/), Sage (https://journals.sagepub.com/) or Taylor and Francis (https://www.tandfonline.com/). The resulting reference list will be checked for duplicates. All unique abstracts will be listed in the XSLX Screening Sheet (see QUEER-SR_Screening_Sheet.xlsx) below and screened for their adherence to the inclusion/exclusion criteria. After this initial screening, in a second phase the full texts of identified articles will be screened again. Any article that does not adhere to each of the inclusion and exclusion criteria listed in this sheet, will be omitted from subsequent extraction procedures. All included articles will be transferred to the data extraction phase (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx).
table.screening_reliability: To allow for the calculation of screener agreement, a proportion of at least 20% of the articles, chosen at random, will be screened by two of the authors to commence each of the two screening phases. Any disagreements across the authors will be discussed until a consensus is reached, based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria.
table.screening_reconciliation_procedure: Disagreement will be resolved in discussion within the author team. Similarly, Abreu et al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022) engaged in multiple meetings to discuss any issues identified during the screening phase.
table.sample_size:
All results from the screening procedure will be sampled resulting from the literature search in journals. The sample size then depends on the number of eligible studies (see above for details). We anticipate to identify between 40 and 60 articles within the 31 listed journals. An informal first search has revealed at least 5 studies, which is the minimum sample size and is expected to be met. 
Leung et al. (2022) initially yielded 565 articles using their search terms. After deduplications were removed, title and abstract screenings revealed 335 articles. Following full article screenings, 128 articles remained. A screening of these 128 articles resulted in 54 articles retained in the review. Abreu et al. (2021) initially identified 694 articles, of which 178 were screened, and of which ultimately 23 were included in the final literature review. No such specifications on the number of articles reviewed were made by Jones et al. (2018).
table.screening_procedure_justification: Our goal is to find all literature on LGBTQ+ issues in the 31 journals listed above. To do this we follow state of the art recommendations with double screening and preregistration of our inclusion and exclusion criteria and procedures.
table.data_management_and_sharing: As exemplified by our screening form, we will share all screened references formatted as an XLSX file online on OSF (see QUEER-SR_Screening_Sheet.xlsx in Screener Instructions). On request, we will share the list of studies that have been double-screened. All coded data will be shared, formatted as an XLSX file online on OSF as exemplified by our coding sheet (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx in Screener Instructions). There are no embargos to be stated. We will share all collected data in an XLSX file on OSF without any embargo when the study is submitted for publication. All original data will be shared together with the materials used during the screening and coding procedure in XLSX files on OSF. This concerns only data relevant to a systematic literature review, since we use no quantitative data as would be the case elsewhere (i.e., in a metaanalysis).
table.miscellaneous_screening_details: No miscellaneous details are to be reported at the present time.
table.entities_to_extract:
As mentioned above, we will screen for original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, and editorials. We will then extract data from the full texts of the identified articles and code characteristics concerning the publication, sample, and design characteristics, as listed below. 

From these articles, we will extract values of dependent variables and potential moderators, on the following publication, sample, and design characteristics if reported:

Publication characteristics:
•	Author team (open field)
•	Title (open field)
•	Reference (open field)
•	Publication year (number)
•	Publication type (journal article; e.g., original research, literature review, opinion paper, commentary, book review, editorial, correction of previously published article)

Sample characteristics
•	Target sample (open field, e.g., queer college students, primary students of LGBTQ+ parents, gay bullying victims, lesbian teachers, etc.)
•	Included sexual orientations (open field)  
•	Included gender identities (open field) 
•	Gender composition (open field)
•	Composition of sexual orientations (open field) 
•	Country of study (open field)
•	Sample size (number)
•	Participants’ mean age (in years) (open field)
•	Age range of the total sample (in years) (open field)
•	Further population subgroup status reported with ethnic, racial, social, religious, or other characteristic different to those from the majority population (yes, no)
	•	If yes, which further population subgroup status was reported? (open field)
•	Grade level (Grade 1 to Grade 12) 
•	Educational level(s) of the sample(s) (Preschool, primary/elementary school, middle school, high school)
•	Type of school (open field)

Design characteristics
•	Design type (Qualitative study; quantitative study; mixed methods)
•	Predictor variables (open field; e.g., bullying, discrimination, etc.)
•	Outcome variables (open field; e.g., school-absenteeism, well-being, etc.)
•	Measurement of predictor variables (open field; e.g., interview, questionnaire, etc.
•	Measurement of outcome variables (open field; e.g., interview, questionnaire, etc.)
	•	If yes, who are the informants of the outcome variables (self, teachers, peers, care-givers, external observers, or combination)
•	Design of study (open field, e.g., cross-sectional, longitudinal, etc.)
•	Possibility to draw causal inferences (yes, no)
•	Open Science adherence adapted from (Emslander et al., 2023; Meyer et al., 2023)
	•	Preregistration (yes, no)
	•	open data (yes, no)
	•	open code (yes, no)
	•	open materials (yes, no)
	•	open access (yes, no)
To judge the quality of the studies and depending on the results of the research identified, we may add other variables (e.g., following new statistics guidelines). We may also judge the transparency of the article and review how measures are described, how the sample is described, and whether a statement on the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) was included. 

Please refer to the Codebook (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx in Extractor Instructions) for more information on how exactly we plan to code these variables.

Similarly, Leung et al. (2022) extracted study characteristics (e.g., study design, school setting, research question), group demographics (e.g., LGBTQ+ acronym, sample size, grade level, age range), and key findings. Due to the research focus, they also identified social support factors, divided into the categories: school support, peer support, parental support, and community support. They also specified school grade range, school type (i.e., catholic, private, democratic) and education level (i.e., elementary, middle, high school). Abreu et al. (2021) extracted study characteristics and demographic information. Additionally, they quantified patterns across studies, either on the experiences of LGBTQ+ students in schools, consequences of oppression on LGBTQ+ students, or on prevention and intervention recommendations (Abreu et al., 2021).
table.extraction_stages:
Similarly to the screening procedure, the first author will extract and review relevant data and variables, 20% of which will be double-coded by another author in parallel. Results will then be discussed with all of us. Thus, extraction will be performed by humans.
After collecting qualitative data fragments and identifying themes of research, we will use these to create clusters and structure the review into chapters (e.g., bullying, support, student outcomes etc.). Jones et al. (2018) identified several themes present within the articles such as: victimization, student outcomes, queer parents, working with teachers, and student support groups. Abreu et al. (2021), Jones et al. (2018), and Leung et al. (2022) conducted thematic analyses of qualitative data to understand the published research and identify patterns (Braun & Clarke, 2006). This method of analysis is often used in reviews as a descriptive, qualitative method to identify themes in the key findings of articles (Braun & Clarke, 2006). We plan to take a similar approach extracting themes of the identified research on LGBTQ+ issues. 

In studies reporting effect sizes, these shall also be extracted. Leung et al. (2022) collected quantitative data on the research design, participant sample size range, LGBTQ+ acronyms used, school setting, number of schools, number of students, and the types of social support.
Depending on the results of the research identified, we may create an evidence gap map, for instance to examine some of the following topics: which age groups or educational levels research has previously focused on, the use of different abbreviations adjacent to “LGBTQ+” throughout literature (see, Leung et al., 2022), inclusion of specific communities within LGBTQ+ people, or themes mentioned around mental health of LGBTQ+ people (e.g., depression, anxiety, minority stress etc.).
table.extractor_instructions: We will go through a training stage, a reliability verification stage, and—if needed—another training stage, and a final extraction stage. First, the first author and one other author will code five studies in a training stage, compare the results, check the interrater agreement, discuss potential problems, and then refine the instructions. We then code the other studies until 20% of studies are double coded. We will randomly choose the studies for double coding. Then, the first author will extract data from the rest of the full texts of the identified articles. Generally, we will code characteristics concerning the publication, sample, and design characteristics, as listed above (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx).
table.extractor_masking: No extractor masking is applied in this study.
table.extraction_reliability: Disagreement will be resolved through discussion after the interrater reliability estimation. The Codebook with a description of all variables and their possible values can be found online (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx). As we cannot completely anticipate which possible variables and their categories will be found, we remain open to the idea of adding further variables to adjust to the present pool of articles after the screening.
table.extraction_reconciliation_procedure: Disagreement will be resolved in discussion within the author team.
table.extraction_procedure_justification: The above-mentioned screening procedures are justified as we follow state of the art recommendations with double coding and preregistration of our exclusion criteria and procedures.
table.miscellaneous_extraction_details: No miscellaneous details are to be reported at the present time.
table.transformations: No data transformations other than the extraction are planned.
table.missing_data_handling: Missing data will be dealt with by mentioning missing variables or effect sizes in articles reviewed. We will critically analyze which data is missing or cannot be obtained and illustrate this and its effects on the systematic literature review during the course of writing.
table.data_validation: After all data has been extracted from the included studies, the first author will perform a plausibility check. If mistakes are noticed we will discuss and correct them.
table.quality_assessment: We will code open science adherence to determine the quality of included articles. As mentioned above, we may also review the quality of the included data by extracting certain variables that determine quality, such as transparency or inclusion of new statistics.
table.synthesis_plan: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.criteria_for_conclusions_inference_crite: To evaluate the sizes of the weighted average effects potentially extracted, we will consider r = .10 to indicate a small effect, r = .20 a medium effect, and r = .30 a large effect (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Gignac & Szodorai, 2016; Paterson et al., 2016) because they are specific to the field of psychology.
table.synthesist_blinding: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_reliability: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_reconciliation_procedure: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.publication_bias_analyses: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.sensitivity_analyses_robustness_checks: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_procedure_justification: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_data_management_and_sharing: As we will be conducting a systematic review, there will be no synthesis data or analytical codes. If we do indeed use analytical code, we will share it online on OSF as an Rmarkdown or SPSS file.
table.miscellaneous_synthesis_details: Part of the present project will be conducted as the work for a master’s thesis at the University of Luxembourg.

table.title: Queering the Pages: A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals [Preregistration]
table.type_of_review: A systematic literature review of published articles, including but not limited to original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials, and corrections of previously published articles.
table.review_stages:
•	October 2023: Preparation of Preregistration
•	November 2023: Preregistration
•	December 2023: Preregistration and Literature Search
•	January 2024: Screening
•	February 2024: Data Extraction
•	March 2024: Critical Appraisal 
•	May and June 2024: Narrative Synthesis
These steps are described in further detail below.
table.current_review_stage: Preregistration and preparation of literature search
table.description:
Interest and subsequent research in the field of LGBTQ+ psychology, that is lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and other non-heterosexual and non-cisgender identities, has increased significantly in recent decades (Walch et al., 2020). In light of this surge, many researchers, publishers, and institutions aim to integrate an LGBTQ+ inclusive approach into their fields of study. Especially in the field of educational psychology, creating an inclusive and safe environment for students at school, is regarded as a necessity for positive student outcomes (Cerezo & Bergfeld, 2013; Fields & Wotipka, 2020). Calls have been made to the field of educational psychology, to increase inclusivity of diverse perspectives relating to sexual orientation and gender identity. As already stated in one such call made by Espelage (2016) in the Journal of School Psychology, a lot of work is yet to be done. 
Indeed, several existing articles in educational psychology journals explore the impact that identifying outside of heterosexual and cisgender norms can have on youth (Abreu et al., 2021; Day et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2020). They illustrate that the process and outcome of a student coming to terms with their LGBTQ+ identity is often mitigated by their school environment, be it peers, teachers, counsellors, or curricula (Abreu et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022). Thus, several factors relating to school experience have been established to determine the well-being of LGBTQ+ students both in their time at school and in later life (Kosciw et al., 2012; Kosciw et al., 2014). Taken together, LGBTQ+ issues in educational psychology are worth investigating to provide instruction on how to create safe environments for both LGBTQ+ students as well as educators, as this is crucial to well-being.
However, this area of research is somewhat underdeveloped in the field of educational
psychology and existing literature in the most cited journals from this field remains sparse. Literature on LGBTQ+ issues is mainly published in LGBTQ+ psychology journals, which in turn emphasize the importance of the inclusion of such topics in educational (or school) psychology (Heck et al., 2016; Snapp et al., 2015). Existing research in educational psychology oftentimes focuses solely on negative themes, such as exclusion, bullying, or discrimination, and their damaging impact on LGBTQ+ students (Birkett et al., 2009; Heck et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2011). 
Large gaps in studies published in educational psychology journals are evident. As such, research on the positive effect of equity and inclusion of LGBTQ+ students in an everyday school environment is less frequent. Thus, the evidence base is scattered, and a comprehensive overview of LGBTQ+ research is needed. Considering this need, a systematic literature review could bring clarity and order into the field. Further, such a systematic review would contribute by reliably illustrating what has already been researched and achieved. At the same time, a systematic review could indicate what is still missing and needs to be explored further, in order to claim that educational psychology is indeed inclusive of LGBTQ+ issues. As such, a scientometric approach will be utilized by the authors of this study. The field of scientometrics concerns itself with measuring and analyzing scholarly literature, including a measurement of the impact of research papers and academic journals (Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012). 
This systematic literature review aims to critically examine the current stance of research on LGBTQ+ issues in schools, in the field of educational psychology. To address the research questions below, we will conduct a systematic review of eligible articles found in 31 of the most cited journals from the field of educational psychology, as illustrated in our search strategy below. To this end, an already existing literature review conducted on this topic by Jones et al. (2018) will be updated and significantly expanded. A further search of similar reviews has revealed two prior articles on LGTBQ+ issues in educational and school psychology (Abreu et al. 2021; Leung et al. 2022). In our systematic literature review, we will address shortcomings of these three literature reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022).
Abreu et al. (2021) reviewed recent literature from 11 school psychology journals, determined as relevant to assess school experiences of LGBTQ+ individuals. The authors identified different themes, such as: oppressive attitudes and behaviors toward LGBTQ+ students and subsequent negative outcomes, LGBTQ+ specific advocacy and support in schools as well as recommendations, LGBTQ+ victimization, bystanders and perpetrators, inclusion policies, and faculty training. The authors maintained an intersectional perspective and focused largely on prevention and intervention practices to create a safe environment in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors reviewed literature published in the field of school psychology only, in order to assess how empirical studies have portrayed the experiences of LGBTQ+ students in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors also chose this approach based on the importance of LGBTQ+ research in the field of school psychology, in laying the groundwork to create affirming spaces for LGBTQ+ students at school. 
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) conducted a systematic search across the disciplines of education and psychology (for more details, see below). They explored existing social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth in schools, using Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992) as an organizational framework. Identified social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate (Leung et al., 2022). The authors illustrated current research on outcomes for LGBTQ+ youth and various barriers to support LGBTQ+ youth in schools (Leung et al., 2022). They also examined how to adapt existing support systems to promote positive outcomes, as well as areas for future research on LGBTQ+ youth (Leung et al., 2022).
In our systematic literature review, we aim to identify current areas of research on LGBTQ+ issues, illustrate where research is missing, state themes future research can expand upon, and highlight how educators can use this information to expand support systems for LGBTQ+ individuals at schools. We will refer to several methods and themes from all three reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022) when conducting the current systematic review. 
The systematic literature review conducted by Abreu et al. (2021) focused on counseling related themes and literature, reviewing empirical studies from the field of school psychology. Moreover, the systematic review conducted by Jones at al. (2018) reviewed all published literature on LGBTQ+ youth in schools from the field of educational psychology, which we will do similarly. However, in comparison to Jones et al. (2018), this systematic review will also broaden the focus beyond LGBTQ+ students and will include LGBTQ+ staff where possible, similarly to the scoping review written by Leung et al. (2022). 
We will take search terms used by Abreu et al. (2021), Jones et al. (2018), and Leung et al. (2022) into account when conducting the literature search. Jones et al. (2018) included research that focused solely on sexual identity minorities. As such, gender minorities are often excluded in research in various fields of psychology, in favor of research on LGB identities (Treadway & Yoakam, 1992; Meyer, 2003; Plöderl & Tremblay, 2015). By including both gender and sexual identity minorities, we will build upon the systematic review by Jones et al. (2018). This entails using many search terms to capture a large variety of identities that are included under the LGBTQ+ umbrella (see Query String below). Methodologically, we will also advance upon the review of Jones et al. (2018). We will document search, screening, and extraction procedures in detail, comparable to Abreu at al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022). Additionally, we will preregister this study to meet open science standards and will conduct a systematic review that is comprehensible to any audience, and can be easily replicated as all material and data will be documented and made publicly available. 
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) organized literature identified into various categories of social support for LGBTQ+ students based on Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992). These categories of social support included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate. Depending on our results, we may examine various support systems in a similar framework, however, we have no intention to conduct our review based on these predetermined support categories. Leung et al. (2022) excluded any research that is unrelated to school environments and where social support outcomes where not related to students (i.e., teachers, parents). Consulting a social science librarian, Leung et al. (2022) followed the methodological scoping review approach designed by Arksey and O’Malley (2007), searching across the disciplines of education and psychology. The purpose of their study was to create a less systematic nevertheless broad overview of social support systems, which was met through this strategy (Leung et al, 2022). A scoping review was also chosen to include both empirical and non-empirical literature, the latter meaning books, book chapters, case reports, and reviews. However, a scoping review search strategy utilizes a less defined search. We will conduct a full systematic literature review using precise search terms listed below. Of note, Leung et al. (2022) analyzed which of the many terms of the LGBTQ+ acronym were used most often and which were used least in existing literature, which we aim to repeat once articles are extracted. We would additionally like to adopt the approach of Leung et al. (2022) to provide a positive outlook on LGBTQ+ youth’s school experiences, however broadening this focus beyond youth to staff and care-givers as mentioned above.
Abreu et al. (2021) identified all studies in the field of school psychology published between 2009 and 2019. Leung et al. (2022) extracted articles published between 2007 and 2021. Similarly to Jones et al. (2018), in our systematic review we will include every article published in the most cited journals of educational psychology, including most recent publications. The latter is important to account for rapid changes in LGBTQ+ populations, that can be observed in the current time.

table.research_questions:
We will examine the following three research questions:

Research Question 1: To what extent is LGBTQ+ centered research represented in the field of educational psychology? 

Research Question 2: What are the common themes and trends in LGBTQ+ centered research in the field of educational psychology thus far?

Research Question 3: Where can major gaps in research on LGBTQ+ topics be identified and subsequently, which topics can future research focus on? Expectation 1: We expect that existing research that focuses on LGBTQ+ issues in educational psychology is sparse and issues are only reported by half of the reviewed journals, similarly to Jones et al. (2018). 

Expectation 2: We expect to find that research focuses mainly on negative aspects related to LGBTQ+ identities in educational contexts (e.g., bullying, discrimination, or exclusion).

Expectation 3: To a lesser extent, we expect to find research on the positive effect of teacher and care-giver support, support groups, and measures taken by schools regarding LGBTQ+ issues. 

Expectation 4: We expect to identify several research gaps in articles published in the relevant journals. Such research gaps could potentially include a focus on negative outcomes, issues only relevant to specific age groups, and more student- compared to teacher-focused research. We aim to showcase a range of future research topics deducted from these research gaps.
table.secondary_research_question_s: Research Question 4: How can the common themes and trends identified be applied to guide educators and care-givers of LGBTQ+ students?

table.databases:
Our literature search will focus on articles published in 31 identified journals from the field of educational psychology. Similarly, to Jones et al. (2018), we will use the most cited journals to receive an accurate portrayal of the field of educational psychology. Jones et al. (2018) identified 21 journals. Abreu et al. (2021) examined articles in 11 school psychology journals. We will use 31 journals, all of which have a Journal Impact Factor in the upper two quartiles in the field of educational psychology. Specifically, with a Journal Impact Factor in the two upper quartiles since 2022 as per SCIMAGO https://jcr-clarivate-com.proxy.bnl.lu/jcr/browse-journals (accessed on November 08th 2023). In accordance with criteria set by us (see inclusion and exclusion criteria below) all relevant articles will be extracted, as this specific scientometric approach has been previously established (see also Fong et al., 2022).
We will search relevant articles including, but not limited to original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials, and corrections of previously published articles, published in the 31 most cited journals educational psychology. table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will include articles which fulfill all of the following criteria:
•	Relevant articles include original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials and corrections of previously published articles
•	We will only include articles published in relevant journals (listed above) 
•	Literature and data found refers to an educational context
•	LGBTQ+ issues are a main topic of the article and are not only discussed or mentioned

We will exclude articles if they fulfill one or more of the following exclusion criteria:
•	For phase one of the search: The abstract or keywords reporting the results of the study are not available
•	For phase two of the search: The full text, or secondary sources reporting the results of the study are not available
•	Search terms are only found in author names
Additionally, overlap between otherwise independent studies will be checked and dealt with after the screening.
table.query_strings:
To ensure a comprehensive, yet specific search, we created our search terms focusing on words that relate to LGBTQ+ identities. Concretely, we provide a selection of LGBTQ+ related words adapted from search terms applied in previous reviews on LGBTQ+ topics (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022). Leung et al. (2022) emphasize that the use of search terms can hinder capturing all identities included in the LGBTQ+ community, particularly gender minority identities. Thus, we will include a wide range of search terms for gender minorities as well as sexual identity minorities. The use of several outdated terms was a deliberate choice made by the authors to identify literature that may originate from a period where such terms were used commonly (e.g., hermaphroditism). 

We will search the titles, abstracts, and keywords of the identified 31 journals with the following search term (example search term in ERIC):

(Sexuality OR sexual minorit* OR gender minorit* OR sexual divers* OR gender divers* OR queer OR LGB* OR GLB* OR 2SLGBTQ+ OR sexual orientation* OR sexual identit* OR gender identit* OR same-sex OR hermaphroditism OR transsexual* OR sapphic OR achillean OR homosexual* OR lesbian* OR gay* OR bisexual* OR demigender* OR bigender* OR agender OR demisexual* OR transgender* OR gender express* OR gender expans* OR gender fluid OR transsexual* OR trans masc* OR trans fem* OR non-binary OR N2 gender-queer OR N2 gender-fluid OR N2 gender non-conforming OR intersexual* OR pansexual* OR asexual* OR aromanti* OR N2 coming-out OR heteronormativ* OR cissex* OR heterorsexis* OR non-heterosexual* OR cisnormativit* OR homophobi* OR transphobi*)

Examples of our screening forms can be found online (see QUEER-SR_Screening_Sheet.xlsx in Screener Instructions).

Both Abreu et al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022) included further search terms, accounting for other areas relevant to research questions. Leung et al (2022) searched LGBTQ+ terms (e.g., homosexuality, bisexuality, gender identity), school related terms (e.g., high school students) and social support terms (e.g., peers). Abreu et al. (2021) searched LGBTQ+ terms (i.e., sexual and gender identity, LGBTQ, GLBTQ, LGB, GLB, queer, gay, homosexuality, male homosexuality, bisexuality, lesbian, trans, transgender, sexual orientation, sexual identity, sexual minority, gender identity, gender expression, gender diversity, gender expansive, genderqueer, and gender fluid),  school related terms (i.e., student, students, alumnus, alumni, former student, and k‐12 students), and school psychology terms (i.e., school psychology, school psychologist(s), and psychology in school(s)). We will focus solely on terms related to the LGBTQ+ umbrella, to identify all articles on LGBTQ+ issues published in the field of educational psychology without restriction.
table.search_validation_procedure: We will validate the search results on ERIC by applying the same search terms on official journal websites and comparing results there, such as APA PsycNet (https://psycnet.apa.org/), Sage (https://journals.sagepub.com/), Taylor and Francis (https://www.tandfonline.com/), or other official journal inventories depending on search results. Any other articles found in only one of either database will be included in the search and later screened and coded.

table.procedures_to_contact_authors: We will contact authors to kindly ask them to provide us with full articles in case we find no access to an article from a relevant journal. If they do not reply within a two-week deadline, we will exclude that article.
table.results_of_contacting_authors: To make sure we have all relevant articles, any articles provided by the contacted authors will be included in the systematic literature review. We will further acknowledge authors for providing us with these full articles.

(2022) had two data collection phases, one in 2017 and a revision in 2021, to account for the many changes happening in society related to LGBTQ+ populations. Only articles which are available at the time of the search, fulfill all our inclusion criteria, and do not meet any of the exclusion criteria, will be included.
table.search_strategy_justification:
This systematic review is conducted to assess the current stance of published articles in journals of educational psychology. Therefore, a search using a database with published journal articles from the field of education shall be utilized. 
The database ERIC is an internet-based bibliographic and full-text database of education research and information. Founded in 1964, ERIC is designed for user groups such as academics, researchers, educators, policymakers, and the general public (https://eric.ed.gov/?faq). Considering this, ERIC is a suitable database to conduct the present systematic review for the field of educational psychology.
table.miscellaneous_search_strategy_details: No miscellaneous details are to be reported at the present time.
table.screening_stages:
We will screen, extract, and review the selected literature, following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, which is an addition to the methods used by Jones et al. (2018) and was also used by Abreu et al. (2021). We anticipate to identify between 40 and 60 articles within the 31 listed journals. The previous study from Leung et al. (2022) identified 54 articles and that of Abreu et al. (2021) identified 23 articles to extract. No such specifications were made by Jones et al. (2018).
The first author will screen and review the literature, and then discuss results with all authors. Two authors will screen at least 20% of the articles. We will use the deduplication feature implemented in Zotero to screen for duplicates. Other duplicates will be identified manually through the screening and coding processes.
table.screened_fields_blinding: We will locate the search terms listed above in titles, abstracts, and keywords of published articles. The first author will search for and screen the literature independently, we will then have one other author double-screen 20% of the findings, and all results will be included in the systematic review; therefore, no blinding is necessary.
table.used_exclusion_criteria:
We will exclude articles during the screening if they fulfill one or more of the following exclusion criteria:
•	For phase one of the search: The abstract or keywords reporting the results of the study are not available
•	For phase two of the search: The full text, or secondary sources reporting the results of the study are not available
•	Search terms are only found in author names
table.screener_instructions: Following PRISMA guidelines, journal articles will be identified in the relevant journals. In a first phase, using the database ERIC, we will collect articles containing search words in titles, abstracts, or in key word sections. Articles found will be cross-validated with online journal inventories, such as APA PsycNet (https://psycnet.apa.org/), Sage (https://journals.sagepub.com/) or Taylor and Francis (https://www.tandfonline.com/). The resulting reference list will be checked for duplicates. All unique abstracts will be listed in the XSLX Screening Sheet (see QUEER-SR_Screening_Sheet.xlsx) below and screened for their adherence to the inclusion/exclusion criteria. After this initial screening, in a second phase the full texts of identified articles will be screened again. Any article that does not adhere to each of the inclusion and exclusion criteria listed in this sheet, will be omitted from subsequent extraction procedures. All included articles will be transferred to the data extraction phase (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx).
table.screening_reliability: To allow for the calculation of screener agreement, a proportion of at least 20% of the articles, chosen at random, will be screened by two of the authors to commence each of the two screening phases. Any disagreements across the authors will be discussed until a consensus is reached, based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria.
table.screening_reconciliation_procedure: Disagreement will be resolved in discussion within the author team. Similarly, Abreu et al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022) engaged in multiple meetings to discuss any issues identified during the screening phase.
table.sample_size:
All results from the screening procedure will be sampled resulting from the literature search in journals. The sample size then depends on the number of eligible studies (see above for details). We anticipate to identify between 40 and 60 articles within the 31 listed journals. An informal first search has revealed at least 5 studies, which is the minimum sample size and is expected to be met. 
Leung et al. (2022) initially yielded 565 articles using their search terms. After deduplications were removed, title and abstract screenings revealed 335 articles. Following full article screenings, 128 articles remained. A screening of these 128 articles resulted in 54 articles retained in the review. Abreu et al. (2021) initially identified 694 articles, of which 178 were screened, and of which ultimately 23 were included in the final literature review. No such specifications on the number of articles reviewed were made by Jones et al. (2018).
table.screening_procedure_justification: Our goal is to find all literature on LGBTQ+ issues in the 31 journals listed above. To do this we follow state of the art recommendations with double screening and preregistration of our inclusion and exclusion criteria and procedures.
table.data_management_and_sharing: As exemplified by our screening form, we will share all screened references formatted as an XLSX file online on OSF (see QUEER-SR_Screening_Sheet.xlsx in Screener Instructions). On request, we will share the list of studies that have been double-screened. All coded data will be shared, formatted as an XLSX file online on OSF as exemplified by our coding sheet (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx in Screener Instructions). There are no embargos to be stated. We will share all collected data in an XLSX file on OSF without any embargo when the study is submitted for publication. All original data will be shared together with the materials used during the screening and coding procedure in XLSX files on OSF. This concerns only data relevant to a systematic literature review, since we use no quantitative data as would be the case elsewhere (i.e., in a metaanalysis).
table.miscellaneous_screening_details: No miscellaneous details are to be reported at the present time.
table.entities_to_extract:
As mentioned above, we will screen for original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, and editorials. We will then extract data from the full texts of the identified articles and code characteristics concerning the publication, sample, and design characteristics, as listed below. 

From these articles, we will extract values of dependent variables and potential moderators, on the following publication, sample, and design characteristics if reported:

Publication characteristics:
•	Author team (open field)
•	Title (open field)
•	Reference (open field)
•	Publication year (number)
•	Publication type (journal article; e.g., original research, literature review, opinion paper, commentary, book review, editorial, correction of previously published article)

Sample characteristics
•	Target sample (open field, e.g., queer college students, primary students of LGBTQ+ parents, gay bullying victims, lesbian teachers, etc.)
•	Included sexual orientations (open field)  
•	Included gender identities (open field) 
•	Gender composition (open field)
•	Composition of sexual orientations (open field) 
•	Country of study (open field)
•	Sample size (number)
•	Participants’ mean age (in years) (open field)
•	Age range of the total sample (in years) (open field)
•	Further population subgroup status reported with ethnic, racial, social, religious, or other characteristic different to those from the majority population (yes, no)
	•	If yes, which further population subgroup status was reported? (open field)
•	Grade level (Grade 1 to Grade 12) 
•	Educational level(s) of the sample(s) (Preschool, primary/elementary school, middle school, high school)
•	Type of school (open field)

Design characteristics
•	Design type (Qualitative study; quantitative study; mixed methods)
•	Predictor variables (open field; e.g., bullying, discrimination, etc.)
•	Outcome variables (open field; e.g., school-absenteeism, well-being, etc.)
•	Measurement of predictor variables (open field; e.g., interview, questionnaire, etc.
•	Measurement of outcome variables (open field; e.g., interview, questionnaire, etc.)
	•	If yes, who are the informants of the outcome variables (self, teachers, peers, care-givers, external observers, or combination)
•	Design of study (open field, e.g., cross-sectional, longitudinal, etc.)
•	Possibility to draw causal inferences (yes, no)
•	Open Science adherence adapted from (Emslander et al., 2023; Meyer et al., 2023)
	•	Preregistration (yes, no)
	•	open data (yes, no)
	•	open code (yes, no)
	•	open materials (yes, no)
	•	open access (yes, no)
To judge the quality of the studies and depending on the results of the research identified, we may add other variables (e.g., following new statistics guidelines). We may also judge the transparency of the article and review how measures are described, how the sample is described, and whether a statement on the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) was included. 

Please refer to the Codebook (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx in Extractor Instructions) for more information on how exactly we plan to code these variables.

Similarly, Leung et al. (2022) extracted study characteristics (e.g., study design, school setting, research question), group demographics (e.g., LGBTQ+ acronym, sample size, grade level, age range), and key findings. Due to the research focus, they also identified social support factors, divided into the categories: school support, peer support, parental support, and community support. They also specified school grade range, school type (i.e., catholic, private, democratic) and education level (i.e., elementary, middle, high school). Abreu et al. (2021) extracted study characteristics and demographic information. Additionally, they quantified patterns across studies, either on the experiences of LGBTQ+ students in schools, consequences of oppression on LGBTQ+ students, or on prevention and intervention recommendations (Abreu et al., 2021).
table.extraction_stages:
Similarly to the screening procedure, the first author will extract and review relevant data and variables, 20% of which will be double-coded by another author in parallel. Results will then be discussed with all of us. Thus, extraction will be performed by humans.
After collecting qualitative data fragments and identifying themes of research, we will use these to create clusters and structure the review into chapters (e.g., bullying, support, student outcomes etc.). Jones et al. (2018) identified several themes present within the articles such as: victimization, student outcomes, queer parents, working with teachers, and student support groups. Abreu et al. (2021), Jones et al. (2018), and Leung et al. (2022) conducted thematic analyses of qualitative data to understand the published research and identify patterns (Braun & Clarke, 2006). This method of analysis is often used in reviews as a descriptive, qualitative method to identify themes in the key findings of articles (Braun & Clarke, 2006). We plan to take a similar approach extracting themes of the identified research on LGBTQ+ issues. 

In studies reporting effect sizes, these shall also be extracted. Leung et al. (2022) collected quantitative data on the research design, participant sample size range, LGBTQ+ acronyms used, school setting, number of schools, number of students, and the types of social support.
Depending on the results of the research identified, we may create an evidence gap map, for instance to examine some of the following topics: which age groups or educational levels research has previously focused on, the use of different abbreviations adjacent to “LGBTQ+” throughout literature (see, Leung et al., 2022), inclusion of specific communities within LGBTQ+ people, or themes mentioned around mental health of LGBTQ+ people (e.g., depression, anxiety, minority stress etc.).
table.extractor_instructions: We will go through a training stage, a reliability verification stage, and—if needed—another training stage, and a final extraction stage. First, the first author and one other author will code five studies in a training stage, compare the results, check the interrater agreement, discuss potential problems, and then refine the instructions. We then code the other studies until 20% of studies are double coded. We will randomly choose the studies for double coding. Then, the first author will extract data from the rest of the full texts of the identified articles. Generally, we will code characteristics concerning the publication, sample, and design characteristics, as listed above (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx).
table.extractor_masking: No extractor masking is applied in this study.
table.extraction_reliability: Disagreement will be resolved through discussion after the interrater reliability estimation. The Codebook with a description of all variables and their possible values can be found online (see QUEER-SR_Codebook.xlsx). As we cannot completely anticipate which possible variables and their categories will be found, we remain open to the idea of adding further variables to adjust to the present pool of articles after the screening.
table.extraction_reconciliation_procedure: Disagreement will be resolved in discussion within the author team.
table.extraction_procedure_justification: The above-mentioned screening procedures are justified as we follow state of the art recommendations with double coding and preregistration of our exclusion criteria and procedures.
table.miscellaneous_extraction_details: No miscellaneous details are to be reported at the present time.
table.transformations: No data transformations other than the extraction are planned.
table.missing_data_handling: Missing data will be dealt with by mentioning missing variables or effect sizes in articles reviewed. We will critically analyze which data is missing or cannot be obtained and illustrate this and its effects on the systematic literature review during the course of writing.
table.data_validation: After all data has been extracted from the included studies, the first author will perform a plausibility check. If mistakes are noticed we will discuss and correct them.
table.quality_assessment: We will code open science adherence to determine the quality of included articles. As mentioned above, we may also review the quality of the included data by extracting certain variables that determine quality, such as transparency or inclusion of new statistics.
table.synthesis_plan: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.criteria_for_conclusions_inference_crite: To evaluate the sizes of the weighted average effects potentially extracted, we will consider r = .10 to indicate a small effect, r = .20 a medium effect, and r = .30 a large effect (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Gignac & Szodorai, 2016; Paterson et al., 2016) because they are specific to the field of psychology.
table.synthesist_blinding: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_reliability: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_reconciliation_procedure: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.publication_bias_analyses: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.sensitivity_analyses_robustness_checks: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_procedure_justification: Not applicable for the present systematic literature review.
table.synthesis_data_management_and_sharing: As we will be conducting a systematic review, there will be no synthesis data or analytical codes. If we do indeed use analytical code, we will share it online on OSF as an Rmarkdown or SPSS file.
table.miscellaneous_synthesis_details: Part of the present project will be conducted as the work for a master’s thesis at the University of Luxembourg.
