These steps are described in further detail below.", "Preregistration and preparation of literature search", "1st October 2023", "1st July 2024", "Interest and subsequent research in the field of LGBTQ+ psychology, that is lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and other non-heterosexual and non-cisgender identities, has increased significantly in recent decades (Walch et al., 2020). In light of this surge, many researchers, publishers, and institutions aim to integrate an LGBTQ+ inclusive approach into their fields of study. Especially in the field of educational psychology, creating an inclusive and safe environment for students at school, is regarded as a necessity for positive student outcomes (Cerezo & Bergfeld, 2013; Fields & Wotipka, 2020). Calls have been made to the field of educational psychology, to increase inclusivity of diverse perspectives relating to sexual orientation and gender identity. As already stated in one such call made by Espelage (2016) in the Journal of School Psychology, a lot of work is yet to be done.
Indeed, several existing articles in educational psychology journals explore the impact that identifying outside of heterosexual and cisgender norms can have on youth (Abreu et al., 2021; Day et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2020). They illustrate that the process and outcome of a student coming to terms with their LGBTQ+ identity is often mitigated by their school environment, be it peers, teachers, counsellors, or curricula (Abreu et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022). Thus, several factors relating to school experience have been established to determine the well-being of LGBTQ+ students both in their time at school and in later life (Kosciw et al., 2012; Kosciw et al., 2014). Taken together, LGBTQ+ issues in educational psychology are worth investigating to provide instruction on how to create safe environments for both LGBTQ+ students as well as educators, as this is crucial to well-being.
However, this area of research is somewhat underdeveloped in the field of educational
psychology and existing literature in the most cited journals from this field remains sparse. Literature on LGBTQ+ issues is mainly published in LGBTQ+ psychology journals, which in turn emphasize the importance of the inclusion of such topics in educational (or school) psychology (Heck et al., 2016; Snapp et al., 2015). Existing research in educational psychology oftentimes focuses solely on negative themes, such as exclusion, bullying, or discrimination, and their damaging impact on LGBTQ+ students (Birkett et al., 2009; Heck et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2011).
Large gaps in studies published in educational psychology journals are evident. As such, research on the positive effect of equity and inclusion of LGBTQ+ students in an everyday school environment is less frequent. Thus, the evidence base is scattered, and a comprehensive overview of LGBTQ+ research is needed. Considering this need, a systematic literature review could bring clarity and order into the field. Further, such a systematic review would contribute by reliably illustrating what has already been researched and achieved. At the same time, a systematic review could indicate what is still missing and needs to be explored further, in order to claim that educational psychology is indeed inclusive of LGBTQ+ issues. As such, a scientometric approach will be utilized by the authors of this study. The field of scientometrics concerns itself with measuring and analyzing scholarly literature, including a measurement of the impact of research papers and academic journals (Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012).
This systematic literature review aims to critically examine the current stance of research on LGBTQ+ issues in schools, in the field of educational psychology. To address the research questions below, we will conduct a systematic review of eligible articles found in 31 of the most cited journals from the field of educational psychology, as illustrated in our search strategy below. To this end, an already existing literature review conducted on this topic by Jones et al. (2018) will be updated and significantly expanded. A further search of similar reviews has revealed two prior articles on LGTBQ+ issues in educational and school psychology (Abreu et al. 2021; Leung et al. 2022). In our systematic literature review, we will address shortcomings of these three literature reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022).
Abreu et al. (2021) reviewed recent literature from 11 school psychology journals, determined as relevant to assess school experiences of LGBTQ+ individuals. The authors identified different themes, such as: oppressive attitudes and behaviors toward LGBTQ+ students and subsequent negative outcomes, LGBTQ+ specific advocacy and support in schools as well as recommendations, LGBTQ+ victimization, bystanders and perpetrators, inclusion policies, and faculty training. The authors maintained an intersectional perspective and focused largely on prevention and intervention practices to create a safe environment in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors reviewed literature published in the field of school psychology only, in order to assess how empirical studies have portrayed the experiences of LGBTQ+ students in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors also chose this approach based on the importance of LGBTQ+ research in the field of school psychology, in laying the groundwork to create affirming spaces for LGBTQ+ students at school.
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) conducted a systematic search across the disciplines of education and psychology (for more details, see below). They explored existing social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth in schools, using Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992) as an organizational framework. Identified social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate (Leung et al., 2022). The authors illustrated current research on outcomes for LGBTQ+ youth and various barriers to support LGBTQ+ youth in schools (Leung et al., 2022). They also examined how to adapt existing support systems to promote positive outcomes, as well as areas for future research on LGBTQ+ youth (Leung et al., 2022).
In our systematic literature review, we aim to identify current areas of research on LGBTQ+ issues, illustrate where research is missing, state themes future research can expand upon, and highlight how educators can use this information to expand support systems for LGBTQ+ individuals at schools. We will refer to several methods and themes from all three reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022) when conducting the current systematic review.
The systematic literature review conducted by Abreu et al. (2021) focused on counseling related themes and literature, reviewing empirical studies from the field of school psychology. Moreover, the systematic review conducted by Jones at al. (2018) reviewed all published literature on LGBTQ+ youth in schools from the field of educational psychology, which we will do similarly. However, in comparison to Jones et al. (2018), this systematic review will also broaden the focus beyond LGBTQ+ students and will include LGBTQ+ staff where possible, similarly to the scoping review written by Leung et al. (2022).
We will take search terms used by Abreu et al. (2021), Jones et al. (2018), and Leung et al. (2022) into account when conducting the literature search. Jones et al. (2018) included research that focused solely on sexual identity minorities. As such, gender minorities are often excluded in research in various fields of psychology, in favor of research on LGB identities (Treadway & Yoakam, 1992; Meyer, 2003; Plöderl & Tremblay, 2015). By including both gender and sexual identity minorities, we will build upon the systematic review by Jones et al. (2018). This entails using many search terms to capture a large variety of identities that are included under the LGBTQ+ umbrella (see Query String below). Methodologically, we will also advance upon the review of Jones et al. (2018). We will document search, screening, and extraction procedures in detail, comparable to Abreu at al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022). Additionally, we will preregister this study to meet open science standards and will conduct a systematic review that is comprehensible to any audience, and can be easily replicated as all material and data will be documented and made publicly available.
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) organized literature identified into various categories of social support for LGBTQ+ students based on Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992). These categories of social support included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate. Depending on our results, we may examine various support systems in a similar framework, however, we have no intention to conduct our review based on these predetermined support categories. Leung et al. (2022) excluded any research that is unrelated to school environments and where social support outcomes where not related to students (i.e., teachers, parents). Consulting a social science librarian, Leung et al. (2022) followed the methodological scoping review approach designed by Arksey and O’Malley (2007), searching across the disciplines of education and psychology. The purpose of their study was to create a less systematic nevertheless broad overview of social support systems, which was met through this strategy (Leung et al, 2022). A scoping review was also chosen to include both empirical and non-empirical literature, the latter meaning books, book chapters, case reports, and reviews. However, a scoping review search strategy utilizes a less defined search. We will conduct a full systematic literature review using precise search terms listed below. Of note, Leung et al. (2022) analyzed which of the many terms of the LGBTQ+ acronym were used most often and which were used least in existing literature, which we aim to repeat once articles are extracted. We would additionally like to adopt the approach of Leung et al. (2022) to provide a positive outlook on LGBTQ+ youth’s school experiences, however broadening this focus beyond youth to staff and care-givers as mentioned above.
Abreu et al. (2021) identified all studies in the field of school psychology published between 2009 and 2019. Leung et al. (2022) extracted articles published between 2007 and 2021. Similarly to Jones et al. (2018), in our systematic review we will include every article published in the most cited journals of educational psychology, including most recent publications. The latter is important to account for rapid changes in LGBTQ+ populations, that can be observed in the current time.

These steps are described in further detail below.", "Preregistration and preparation of literature search", "1st October 2023", "1st July 2024", "Interest and subsequent research in the field of LGBTQ+ psychology, that is lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and other non-heterosexual and non-cisgender identities, has increased significantly in recent decades (Walch et al., 2020). In light of this surge, many researchers, publishers, and institutions aim to integrate an LGBTQ+ inclusive approach into their fields of study. Especially in the field of educational psychology, creating an inclusive and safe environment for students at school, is regarded as a necessity for positive student outcomes (Cerezo & Bergfeld, 2013; Fields & Wotipka, 2020). Calls have been made to the field of educational psychology, to increase inclusivity of diverse perspectives relating to sexual orientation and gender identity. As already stated in one such call made by Espelage (2016) in the Journal of School Psychology, a lot of work is yet to be done.
Indeed, several existing articles in educational psychology journals explore the impact that identifying outside of heterosexual and cisgender norms can have on youth (Abreu et al., 2021; Day et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2020). They illustrate that the process and outcome of a student coming to terms with their LGBTQ+ identity is often mitigated by their school environment, be it peers, teachers, counsellors, or curricula (Abreu et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022). Thus, several factors relating to school experience have been established to determine the well-being of LGBTQ+ students both in their time at school and in later life (Kosciw et al., 2012; Kosciw et al., 2014). Taken together, LGBTQ+ issues in educational psychology are worth investigating to provide instruction on how to create safe environments for both LGBTQ+ students as well as educators, as this is crucial to well-being.
However, this area of research is somewhat underdeveloped in the field of educational
psychology and existing literature in the most cited journals from this field remains sparse. Literature on LGBTQ+ issues is mainly published in LGBTQ+ psychology journals, which in turn emphasize the importance of the inclusion of such topics in educational (or school) psychology (Heck et al., 2016; Snapp et al., 2015). Existing research in educational psychology oftentimes focuses solely on negative themes, such as exclusion, bullying, or discrimination, and their damaging impact on LGBTQ+ students (Birkett et al., 2009; Heck et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2011).
Large gaps in studies published in educational psychology journals are evident. As such, research on the positive effect of equity and inclusion of LGBTQ+ students in an everyday school environment is less frequent. Thus, the evidence base is scattered, and a comprehensive overview of LGBTQ+ research is needed. Considering this need, a systematic literature review could bring clarity and order into the field. Further, such a systematic review would contribute by reliably illustrating what has already been researched and achieved. At the same time, a systematic review could indicate what is still missing and needs to be explored further, in order to claim that educational psychology is indeed inclusive of LGBTQ+ issues. As such, a scientometric approach will be utilized by the authors of this study. The field of scientometrics concerns itself with measuring and analyzing scholarly literature, including a measurement of the impact of research papers and academic journals (Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012).
This systematic literature review aims to critically examine the current stance of research on LGBTQ+ issues in schools, in the field of educational psychology. To address the research questions below, we will conduct a systematic review of eligible articles found in 31 of the most cited journals from the field of educational psychology, as illustrated in our search strategy below. To this end, an already existing literature review conducted on this topic by Jones et al. (2018) will be updated and significantly expanded. A further search of similar reviews has revealed two prior articles on LGTBQ+ issues in educational and school psychology (Abreu et al. 2021; Leung et al. 2022). In our systematic literature review, we will address shortcomings of these three literature reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022).
Abreu et al. (2021) reviewed recent literature from 11 school psychology journals, determined as relevant to assess school experiences of LGBTQ+ individuals. The authors identified different themes, such as: oppressive attitudes and behaviors toward LGBTQ+ students and subsequent negative outcomes, LGBTQ+ specific advocacy and support in schools as well as recommendations, LGBTQ+ victimization, bystanders and perpetrators, inclusion policies, and faculty training. The authors maintained an intersectional perspective and focused largely on prevention and intervention practices to create a safe environment in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors reviewed literature published in the field of school psychology only, in order to assess how empirical studies have portrayed the experiences of LGBTQ+ students in schools (Abreu et al., 2021). The authors also chose this approach based on the importance of LGBTQ+ research in the field of school psychology, in laying the groundwork to create affirming spaces for LGBTQ+ students at school.
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) conducted a systematic search across the disciplines of education and psychology (for more details, see below). They explored existing social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth in schools, using Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992) as an organizational framework. Identified social support systems for LGBTQ+ youth included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate (Leung et al., 2022). The authors illustrated current research on outcomes for LGBTQ+ youth and various barriers to support LGBTQ+ youth in schools (Leung et al., 2022). They also examined how to adapt existing support systems to promote positive outcomes, as well as areas for future research on LGBTQ+ youth (Leung et al., 2022).
In our systematic literature review, we aim to identify current areas of research on LGBTQ+ issues, illustrate where research is missing, state themes future research can expand upon, and highlight how educators can use this information to expand support systems for LGBTQ+ individuals at schools. We will refer to several methods and themes from all three reviews (i.e., Abreu et al., 2021; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022) when conducting the current systematic review.
The systematic literature review conducted by Abreu et al. (2021) focused on counseling related themes and literature, reviewing empirical studies from the field of school psychology. Moreover, the systematic review conducted by Jones at al. (2018) reviewed all published literature on LGBTQ+ youth in schools from the field of educational psychology, which we will do similarly. However, in comparison to Jones et al. (2018), this systematic review will also broaden the focus beyond LGBTQ+ students and will include LGBTQ+ staff where possible, similarly to the scoping review written by Leung et al. (2022).
We will take search terms used by Abreu et al. (2021), Jones et al. (2018), and Leung et al. (2022) into account when conducting the literature search. Jones et al. (2018) included research that focused solely on sexual identity minorities. As such, gender minorities are often excluded in research in various fields of psychology, in favor of research on LGB identities (Treadway & Yoakam, 1992; Meyer, 2003; Plöderl & Tremblay, 2015). By including both gender and sexual identity minorities, we will build upon the systematic review by Jones et al. (2018). This entails using many search terms to capture a large variety of identities that are included under the LGBTQ+ umbrella (see Query String below). Methodologically, we will also advance upon the review of Jones et al. (2018). We will document search, screening, and extraction procedures in detail, comparable to Abreu at al. (2021) and Leung et al. (2022). Additionally, we will preregister this study to meet open science standards and will conduct a systematic review that is comprehensible to any audience, and can be easily replicated as all material and data will be documented and made publicly available.
In their scoping review, Leung et al. (2022) organized literature identified into various categories of social support for LGBTQ+ students based on Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory (1992). These categories of social support included: care-givers, curriculum, school professionals and teachers, peers, Gay-Straight-Alliances and programs, school policies, and school climate. Depending on our results, we may examine various support systems in a similar framework, however, we have no intention to conduct our review based on these predetermined support categories. Leung et al. (2022) excluded any research that is unrelated to school environments and where social support outcomes where not related to students (i.e., teachers, parents). Consulting a social science librarian, Leung et al. (2022) followed the methodological scoping review approach designed by Arksey and O’Malley (2007), searching across the disciplines of education and psychology. The purpose of their study was to create a less systematic nevertheless broad overview of social support systems, which was met through this strategy (Leung et al, 2022). A scoping review was also chosen to include both empirical and non-empirical literature, the latter meaning books, book chapters, case reports, and reviews. However, a scoping review search strategy utilizes a less defined search. We will conduct a full systematic literature review using precise search terms listed below. Of note, Leung et al. (2022) analyzed which of the many terms of the LGBTQ+ acronym were used most often and which were used least in existing literature, which we aim to repeat once articles are extracted. We would additionally like to adopt the approach of Leung et al. (2022) to provide a positive outlook on LGBTQ+ youth’s school experiences, however broadening this focus beyond youth to staff and care-givers as mentioned above.
Abreu et al. (2021) identified all studies in the field of school psychology published between 2009 and 2019. Leung et al. (2022) extracted articles published between 2007 and 2021. Similarly to Jones et al. (2018), in our systematic review we will include every article published in the most cited journals of educational psychology, including most recent publications. The latter is important to account for rapid changes in LGBTQ+ populations, that can be observed in the current time.

We plan to take a similar approach extracting themes of the identified research on LGBTQ+ issues.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 36 columns across 1 data file.
#### Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Publication status: This manuscript is a preprint and has not yet undergone a scientific peer-review process.
It is submitted for publication.

The number of publications on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or other sexual or gender minority identity (LGBTQ+) populations has increased significantly in recent decades (Walch et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The number of publications on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or other sexual or gender minority identity (LGBTQ+) populations has increased significantly in recent decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Walch et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This surge aligns with growing societal acceptance of LGBTQ+ issues and the need for researchers, publishers, and institutions to integrate these issues into their fields of study.

In Educational Psychology, for instance, this can mean creating educational settings that are safe and inclusive for LGBTQ+ students and teachers (Cerezo & Bergfeld, 2013; Fields & Wotipka, 2022; K. Russell, 2021), examining the psychological impact of coming out as LGBTQ+ on youth (Abreu et al., 2022; Day et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2020), or investigating how peers, teachers, counselors, curricula, or other environmental factors influence the well-being of LGBTQ+ students (Kosciw et al., 2013 (Kosciw et al., , 2015)).
text.formatted: In Educational Psychology, for instance, this can mean creating educational settings that are safe and inclusive for LGBTQ+ students and teachers <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cerezo & Bergfeld, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Fields & Wotipka, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">K. Russell, 2021)</ref>, examining the psychological impact of coming out as LGBTQ+ on youth <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abreu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Day et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Myers et al., 2020)</ref>, or investigating how peers, teachers, counselors, curricula, or other environmental factors influence the well-being of LGBTQ+ students <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Kosciw et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Kosciw et al., , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: These and other LGBTQ+ specific issues underscore the need for appropriate support grounded in a wide range of research and for the representation of LGBTQ+ people and their issues in Educational Psychology.

The need to represent LGBTQ+ issues in research is further supported by the growing number of people identifying as anything other than heterosexual or cisgender, who are more likely to report negative school experiences.

Whereas there are no official statistics on the number of LGBTQ+ people in the population for good reasons (see Savin-Williams, 2006), we have large or even representative datasets of self-reported sexual orientation and gender identity that we can use to approximate this number.
text.formatted: Whereas there are no official statistics on the number of LGBTQ+ people in the population for good reasons (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Savin-Williams, 2006)</ref>, we have large or even representative datasets of self-reported sexual orientation and gender identity that we can use to approximate this number.

text.text: A 2021 U.S. Gallup survey (Gallup, 2022) found that 21% of Gen Z Americans (born in 1997 or later) identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or trans, compared with 10.5% of Millennials (born 1981 Millennials (born -1996)).
text.formatted: A 2021 U.S. Gallup survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Gallup, 2022)</ref> found that 21% of Gen Z Americans (born in 1997 or later) identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or trans, compared with 10.5% of <ref type="bibr">Millennials (born 1981</ref> <ref type="bibr">Millennials (born -1996))</ref>.

text.text: These youth often face adversity and discrimination, including in schools.

The National School Climate Survey (Kosciw et al., 2022) reported that 50.6% of LGBTQ+ students felt unsafe at school because of their sexual orientation and gender identity, leading many to avoid school activities or skip days.
text.formatted: The National School Climate Survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Kosciw et al., 2022)</ref> reported that 50.6% of LGBTQ+ students felt unsafe at school because of their sexual orientation and gender identity, leading many to avoid school activities or skip days.

text.text: Additionally, 60.7% experienced verbal harassment, and 22.4% faced physical harassment (Kosciw et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Additionally, 60.7% experienced verbal harassment, and 22.4% faced physical harassment <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Kosciw et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A similar European study of more than 93,000 lesbian, gay, bisexual, or trans people ages 18 or older (European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, 2014) found that 47% reported discrimination in the past year, with young lesbian women most affected.
Younger lesbian, gay, bisexual, or trans people (18-24) reported higher rates of discrimination (57%) than older groups (45% for 25-39 and 38% for 40-54).
In educational settings, 18% felt harassed by staff, and 67% hid their sexual orientation, with only 4% being open about it (European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, 2014).
These figures underscore the need to research LGBTQ+ issues in educational contexts to support learners and staff.
To investigate LGBTQ+ representation in the scientific field of Educational Psychology, we drew on the most-cited Educational Psychology journals in this systematic scientometric review.
In scientometrics, research and publications-including their frequency, impact, trends, and content-are the subjects of investigation (Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012; López-Pernas et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In scientometrics, research and publications-including their frequency, impact, trends, and content-are the subjects of investigation <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">López-Pernas et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: To yield a high-impact sample for this review, we selected all 31 journals from the top two quartiles (Q1 and Q2) of the 2022 Web of Science Journal Citation Reports for the field of Educational Psychology, using the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) as the primary metric (Clarivate, 2024; Garfield, 1999).
text.formatted: To yield a high-impact sample for this review, we selected all 31 journals from the top two quartiles (Q1 and Q2) of the 2022 Web of Science Journal Citation Reports for the field of Educational Psychology, using the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) as the primary metric <ref type="bibr">(Clarivate, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Garfield, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, we apply scientometric methods to quantify LGBTQ+ centered publications, cluster their content using thematic content analysis, and identify research gaps to advance LGBTQ+ centered evidence in Educational Psychology.

Despite the growing number of students, teachers, and caregivers identifying as LGBTQ+ and the need to investigate their issues in educational settings, it remains unclear whether LGBTQ+ representation reaches the most-cited journals in Educational Psychology. Jones et al. (2018) predicted that LGBTQ+ issues are reported in only about half of Educational Psychology journals.
text.formatted: Despite the growing number of students, teachers, and caregivers identifying as LGBTQ+ and the need to investigate their issues in educational settings, it remains unclear whether LGBTQ+ representation reaches the most-cited journals in Educational Psychology. <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Jones et al. (2018)</ref> predicted that LGBTQ+ issues are reported in only about half of Educational Psychology journals.

text.text: They conducted a literature review of 21 Educational Psychology journals from the top 30 by impact factor in 2015. Graybill & Proctor (2016) summarize three major reasons for this scarcity in their review of LGBTQ+ representation in school support personnel journals.
text.formatted: They conducted a literature review of 21 Educational Psychology journals from the top 30 by impact factor in 2015. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Graybill & Proctor (2016)</ref> summarize three major reasons for this scarcity in their review of LGBTQ+ representation in school support personnel journals.

text.text: First, recruitment is challenging because of the difficulty in identifying LGBTQ+ participants and their reluctance due to research fatigue (Worthington & Navarro, 2003).
text.formatted: First, recruitment is challenging because of the difficulty in identifying LGBTQ+ participants and their reluctance due to research fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Worthington & Navarro, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Second, publication patterns suggest that authors may prefer specialized LGBTQ+ journals over general discipline journals because they are perceived as more friendly and receptive (Scherrer & Woodford, 2013).
text.formatted: Second, publication patterns suggest that authors may prefer specialized LGBTQ+ journals over general discipline journals because they are perceived as more friendly and receptive <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">(Scherrer & Woodford, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Third, these trends might reflect a historical landscape marked by the systemic exclusion of LGBTQ+ representation from legal and civil protections (Hackimer & Proctor, 2015).
text.formatted: Third, these trends might reflect a historical landscape marked by the systemic exclusion of LGBTQ+ representation from legal and civil protections <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Hackimer & Proctor, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: But what is the state of LGBTQ+ representation, and how can we investigate it?
LGBTQ+ representation can be examined both quantitatively and qualitatively.

Quantitatively, we can, for example, (1) count publications to gauge the volume and the percentage of total published papers in the field that address LGBTQ+ issues, as done in neighboring fields (e.g., Graybill & Proctor, 2016).
text.formatted: Quantitatively, we can, for example, (1) count publications to gauge the volume and the percentage of total published papers in the field that address LGBTQ+ issues, as done in neighboring fields (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Graybill & Proctor, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we can assess temporal trendswhether the percentage or the number of publications has changed over time.

While research on LGBTQ+ people and issues has increased in recent years (Walch et al., 2020), it remains unclear whether this increase has reached the most-cited Educational Psychology journals in terms of citations and what the drivers of this increase might be.
text.formatted: While research on LGBTQ+ people and issues has increased in recent years <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Walch et al., 2020)</ref>, it remains unclear whether this increase has reached the most-cited Educational Psychology journals in terms of citations and what the drivers of this increase might be.

text.text: Beyond looking at publication figures and percentages, we can (2) investigate differences in publication types and design methods used.

Because it is difficult to obtain a large or even representative sample of LGBTQ+ people (Worthington & Navarro, 2003), original research articles may be published less often in the most-cited Educational Psychology journals, because they require large samples.
text.formatted: Because it is difficult to obtain a large or even representative sample of LGBTQ+ people <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Worthington & Navarro, 2003)</ref>, original research articles may be published less often in the most-cited Educational Psychology journals, because they require large samples.

text.text: Thus, research syntheses might be easier to place in such journals, circumventing the small-sample problem (see above).
Finally, we can (3) examine the distribution of LGBTQ+ participants and authors worldwide.
An analysis of participant demographics can reveal whether samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) countries (Henrich et al., 2010) are overrepresented.
text.formatted: An analysis of participant demographics can reveal whether samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Henrich et al., 2010)</ref> are overrepresented.

text.text: Similarly, we can investigate whether certain LGBTQ+ subgroups, such as gay cisgender men, are studied more frequently than others, such as transgender women or asexual individuals.
As for the authors, the field is likely to be dominated by author teams from North America or Europe, as in other psychological disciplines (e.g., Adair & Huynh, 2012).
text.formatted: As for the authors, the field is likely to be dominated by author teams from North America or Europe, as in other psychological disciplines (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Adair & Huynh, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying these variances is necessary to assess the generalizability of representation across world regions and LGBTQ+ communities.
Quantitative examination of LGBTQ+ representation is particularly interesting in the most impactful scientific journals, defined as those in the top two quartiles of the impact factor ranking.
These journals rank highly by impact factor, the mean number of citations per article in recent years.
This suggests they are the most widely cited and, plausibly, the most read journals in the field.
Therefore, these journals could increase the visibility of the issues and samples they publish and, subsequently, help shape policy, practice, and future research agendas.

Thus, several researchers have called for more research on LGBTQ+ issues to be published in such journals. Espelage (2016) and Graybill et al. (2009) emphasized the need for more research on LGBTQ+ issues, with the latter noting that less than 0.05% of research in their search addressed them.

(2009)</ref> emphasized the need for more research on LGBTQ+ issues, with the latter noting that less than 0.05% of research in their search addressed them.

text.text: However, the literature in psychological science on LGBTQ+ issues is often limited to journals specialized in LGBTQ+ psychology, such as the Journal of Homosexuality (Walch et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, the literature in psychological science on LGBTQ+ issues is often limited to journals specialized in LGBTQ+ psychology, such as the Journal of Homosexuality <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Walch et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas these journals may have a high impact factor in their own right, they are arguably less visible and less widely read within the Educational Psychology community.
This underscores the importance of publishing such topics in general educational (or school) psychology research (Heck et al., 2016; Snapp et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This underscores the importance of publishing such topics in general educational (or school) psychology research <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Heck et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Snapp et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Doing so would increase visibility, advance LGBTQ+ issues by moving them from special-interest topics to the forefront, and fill pressing research gaps with novel insights.

From a historical perspective, other researchers are optimistic about LGBTQ+ representation in academic journals. Mallinckrodt (2009) identified a recent advance in research on lesbian women and gay men, evident in specific journals. Griffin and Ouellett (2003) found in their historical overview that educators' perceptions and subsequent inclusion of LGBTQ+ people have improved over the past several decades.

text.text: Furthermore, organizations such as the National Association of School Psychologists (2020) have issued position statements on LGBTQ+ students in the U.S., and publishers such as Springer have made diversity pledges (Springer Nature, 2025).
text.formatted: Furthermore, organizations such as the National Association of School Psychologists (2020) have issued position statements on LGBTQ+ students in the U.S., and publishers such as Springer have made diversity pledges <ref type="bibr">(Springer Nature, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It remains unclear, however, whether these calls to include more
LGBTQ+ issues in research and diversity pledges translate into publications in the most-cited journals.
Additionally, it is uncertain whether the trend of increasing LGBTQ+ acceptance will continue, given recent changes in the political climate toward LGBTQ+ people in the U.S. and worldwide.
Here, a systematic scientometric review can provide clarity.

Scientometrics is the quantitative "science of science," focusing on evaluating and understanding scientific research and communication (Mingers & Leydesdorff, 2015), making it a comprehensive method to "help understand, map, and summarize scientific research" (López-Pernas et al., 2023, p. 79).

text.text: This approach allowed for a quantitative assessment of LGBTQ+ representation in the mostcited Educational Psychology journals to address several open research gaps.

Our method combines the strengths of a systematic review with those of a scientometric study by following a rigorous protocol to search and evaluate the literature and objectively assess LGBTQ+ representation in most-cited Educational Psychology journals.
In addition to supposed scarcity, quantitative research and measurement with LGBTQ+ populations have faced several issues, including a lack of causal study designs and poor scale design.

First, common study designs in LGBTQ+ centered psychology seem to be almost exclusively non-experimental, descriptive, or observational, often relying on retrospective, cross-sectional, or correlational designs (Walch et al., 2020).
text.formatted: First, common study designs in LGBTQ+ centered psychology seem to be almost exclusively non-experimental, descriptive, or observational, often relying on retrospective, cross-sectional, or correlational designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(Walch et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, much empirical research draws on community-based samples, which can introduce sociodemographic discrepancies (Krueger et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Second, much empirical research draws on community-based samples, which can introduce sociodemographic discrepancies <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Krueger et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Paradoxically, although such studies are better equipped to assess population-specific concerns, they lack generalizability (Krueger et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Paradoxically, although such studies are better equipped to assess population-specific concerns, they lack generalizability <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Krueger et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Third, survey designs seldom offer sexual orientation categories beyond heterosexual, homosexual, and bisexual, and often lack clear differentiation between sex and gender or items to assess intersectionality (Consolacion et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Third, survey designs seldom offer sexual orientation categories beyond heterosexual, homosexual, and bisexual, and often lack clear differentiation between sex and gender or items to assess intersectionality <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Consolacion et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, obtaining valid measurements can be difficult when dealing with sensitive variables like LGBTQ+ identity.
Some participants may choose not to disclose this information, while others may be unable to, which can introduce error and distort the results (see Macapagal et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Some participants may choose not to disclose this information, while others may be unable to, which can introduce error and distort the results (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Macapagal et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, we will quantitatively assess the current state of these methodological issues in LGBTQ+ research in the most-cited journals of Educational Psychology.

Qualitatively, LGBTQ+ representation in Educational Psychology research can be evaluated by (1) the themes of the published articles and (2) whether these themes are strengthoriented (positive) or deficit-oriented (negative).

More specifically, using qualitative thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), we can identify common themes in the current literature and categorize them, pointing at a strength-or deficit-oriented view of LGBTQ+ people and their issues in Educational Psychology.

text.text: In their thematic analysis, Jones et al. (2018) identified the themes victimization, student outcomes, queer parents, working with teachers, and student support groups, which could not be clearly separated into strength-and deficit-oriented themes.

text.text: The present systematic review addresses this issue by deducing themes that are clearly either strength-or deficit-oriented.

Research on LGBTQ+ issues appears limited to a narrow set of mostly deficit-oriented topics, such as bullying, discrimination, and the exclusion of LGBTQ+ youth (Birkett et al., 2009; Espelage et al., 2019; Heck et al., 2014; Myers et al., 2020; S. T. Russell et al., 2011).

text.text: As Savin-Williams (2001) argues, much of the literature focuses on suicide attempts, substance use, and HIV infection rates among sexual minority-identified youth, with less attention to aspects of their daily lives.

This dominant discourse linking LGBTQ+ people with deficitoriented issues shaped educators' understanding of LGBTQ+ students, perhaps to a more negative degree than is constructive (Payne & Smith, 2013).

text.text: Similarly, McCabe and Anhalt (2022) underscore the need to shift this negative narrative and to focus more on the intersecting identities of LGBTQ+ youth.
Consequently, research on the positive effects of equity and inclusion for LGBTQ+ students in everyday school environments is less frequent.

Whereas research on the risks and challenges faced by LGBTQ+ students exists, other LGBTQ+ populations, such as caregivers or teachers involved in educational contexts, are widely disregarded (Abreu et al., 2022; M. H. Jones et al., 2018; Wimberly, 2015).

text.text: To quantify LGBTQ+ representation across both topics and educational settings, we apply Hattie's (2009) taxonomy of educational settings.

text.text: In his seminal systematic meta-metaanalyses, he identified seven settings pertinent to learning: Students, Schools, Classrooms, Teachers, Home, Curriculum, and Learning.
These categories highlight that a wide range of settings are relevant to LGBTQ+ research in Educational Psychology.
When focusing on the individual student, a supportive peer network can play a decisive role (Leung et al., 2022).

text.text: LGBTQ+ students can receive support and understanding from peers with lived experience of the community.
Other protective factors include personality traits, such as hopefulness, self-esteem, and resilience (A. Boyd & Jeffries, 2018; Gray, 2023; Taylor et al., 2017).

text.text: As such, teacher and peer support can benefit LGBTQ+ people experiencing adversity.
Additionally, school support personnel, such as counselors, play a critical role, especially for LGBTQ+ youth in schools (Graybill & Proctor, 2016).

Similarly, support may come from other adults involved in formal education institutions or, perhaps most importantly, from caregivers at home (Espelage et al., 2019).

text.text: Ultimately, knowledge about LGBTQ+ issues, presented to students and school personnel in an approachable manner, can lay the groundwork for supporting and promoting the well-being of LGBTQ+ people in educational settings.

Thus, we will conclude our systematic review with a discussion of avenues for future research to address the pertinent gaps in the most-cited Educational Psychology journals across the diverse educational settings mentioned above.

To examine the representation of LGBTQ+ issues in Educational Psychology and the field's research strands and gaps, the present study reviews all publications available in ERIC in the leading journals in the field, as defined in the Web of Science Journal Citation Reports (Clarivate, 2024).

More specifically, we apply a quantitative, scientometric, and systematic review approach, accompanied by qualitative thematic analyses of the journals in the upper two quartiles in the Web of Science Journal Citation Reports (Clarivate, 2024) for the field of Educational Psychology, resulting in 31 Educational Psychology journals, comparable to the approach of Graybill and Proctor (2016) and Jones et al. (2018).

text.text: The present systematic scientometric literature review combines a large database, rigorous systematic review methods, and a broad scope to provide an overview of the representation of LGBTQ+ issues in Educational Psychology.
Specifically, we address the following research questions (RQs):
LGBTQ+ centered research represented in the most-cited journals of Educational Psychology?
a.
Are there temporal trends?
b.
Which publication types are most/least common?
c.
Which methods are used most/least often?
d.
Which samples are included?
e.
How were gender and sexual orientation assessed and reported?
f.
Which educational stakeholders are most/least researched?
RQ 2: What are the common themes in LGBTQ+ centered research in the most-cited Educational Psychology journals?
a.
Which common themes make it into the top journals?
b.
Does the research focus more on strength-oriented (positive) or deficitoriented (negative) themes?
We preregistered all hypotheses, research questions, and methods (see the Open Science and Transparency statement below).
We addressed RQ 1 by presenting quantitative findings on the representation of LGBTQ+ research in the included articles from the 31 most impactful Educational Psychology journals.
We addressed RQ 2 through a qualitative thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006) of common themes in the included articles.
text.formatted: We addressed RQ 2 through a qualitative thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Braun & Clarke, 2006)</ref> of common themes in the included articles.

text.text: Diverging from our preregistration, we will discuss publication trends alongside RQ 1 and address the preregistered RQ 3, "Where can major gaps in research on LGBTQ+ topics be identified and, subsequently, which topics can future research focus on?"
in the Discussion.

As with previous reviews of related research questions (e.g., Jones et al., 2018), we expect that articles addressing LGBTQ+ topics are rarely published in the 31 most highly cited Educational Psychology journals, that about half of these journals have not published on LGBTQ+ topics to date, and that articles on deficit-oriented LGBTQ+ topics (e.g., homophobic bullying and victimization) are published more frequently than articles on resource-oriented LGBTQ+ topics (e.g., LGBTQ+ advocacy in schools).

To gauge representation and impact, we selected our sample of journals based on Journal Impact Factor (JIF) metrics to comprehensively address the research questions concerning all Educational Psychology publications.

text.text: Within these journals, we searched all issues since each journal's inception using a standardized search term to provide an objective portrayal of the literature covering LGBTQ+ related issues.

All journal article types included in the review were either original research, literature reviews, opinion papers, commentaries, book reviews, editorials, or corrections of previously published articles.
In this review, we use the term article to refer to all types of literature identified.
The articles had to be published in the 31 journals listed in Table 1.

text.text: concerned with research, teaching, or practice in educational settings at all levels (American Psychological Association, n.d.).
LGBTQ+ issues had to be a main topic of the article and not only briefly discussed or mentioned.
The abstract or keywords of the article had to be available for the screening, and the full text or secondary sources reporting the results of the study had to be available for the coding.
Search terms had to be found somewhere in the published document other than in authors' names (e.g., irrelevant articles authored by a person with the last name Gay were excluded).
The second and third authors conducted the screening.
We resolved conflicts through discussion among all three authors.
In the first step, we screened the titles, abstracts, and keywords of all 1,061 articles against a set of inclusion and exclusion criteria.
We conducted training sessions with 5% (i.e., 50) and 10% (i.e., 100) of the articles, which were randomly selected.
The second and third authors screened these articles independently, and the results were then compared.
The two authors achieved almost perfect inter-rater reliability, κ = 0.83, 95% CI [0.80, 0.87] (Landis & Koch, 1977).

text.text: Thus, the second author screened the titles, abstracts, and keywords of all remaining articles independently.
Eighty articles were identified as potentially fitting all our inclusion and exclusion criteria and submitted to the full-text screening.
In the second step, we conducted a full-text screening.
Two training sessions on 10% (i.e., 8) of the articles yielded almost perfect inter-rater reliability of κ = 0.90, 95% CI [0.72, 1.00], between the second and third authors (Landis & Koch, 1977).

text.text: Specifically, we coded characteristics related to the publication, sample, and design, as reported and relevant.

Sample characteristics included the type of sample, the recorded compositions of gender identities and sexual orientations, the country of study, the education level, and other sample-specific characteristics.

Design characteristics included the study design and type, all measured variables (i.e., predictor, mediator, moderator, and outcome variables), the possibility of drawing causal inference, open science adherence, and other factors (see the Codebook in Table S1).

text.text: Missing data were coded as not reported or not applicable.
The research synthesis of findings consisted of two approaches (for similar approaches, see Abreu et al., 2022; M. H. Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2022).

text.text: First, we used a quantitative scientometric approach (López-Pernas et al., 2023) and analyzed data to describe the sample groups and other relevant characteristics.
text.formatted: First, we used a quantitative scientometric approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(López-Pernas et al., 2023)</ref> and analyzed data to describe the sample groups and other relevant characteristics.

text.text: Second, we used thematic analysis to identify common themes to address our research questions.

In our systematic review, we used scientometric techniques to map and evaluate the quantitative representation of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology, following a five-step framework (López-Pernas et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In our systematic review, we used scientometric techniques to map and evaluate the quantitative representation of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology, following a five-step framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(López-Pernas et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: First, we retrieved the data by systematically searching relevant databases to gather necessary metadata and verifying its integrity (see above).
Second, we screened the data for eligibility, ensuring that only pertinent records were included (see above).
Third, during data pre-processing, we addressed inconsistencies, such as variations in author names.
Fourth, we analyzed the data to uncover insights into the research field, including productivity by country and thematic patterns.

Finally, we conducted an integrity check by reviewing the results to verify their alignment with the field's actual state, ensuring that our findings were both robust and representative (for a similar approach, see e.g., Krampen & Hasselhorn, 2019).
text.formatted: Finally, we conducted an integrity check by reviewing the results to verify their alignment with the field's actual state, ensuring that our findings were both robust and representative (for a similar approach, see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Krampen & Hasselhorn, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This approach allowed us to capture a snapshot of LGBTQ+ representation in the most recognized Educational Psychology journals (in terms of citations) and to address RQ 1 on the quantity of LGBTQ+ related publications and preregistered RQ 3 on gaps in the literature of this field.

Thematic analysis, as outlined by Braun and Clarke (2006), is a qualitative method used in reviews to identify themes in key findings and to construct themes and subthemes on specific societal issues.
text.formatted: Thematic analysis, as outlined by <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Braun and Clarke (2006)</ref>, is a qualitative method used in reviews to identify themes in key findings and to construct themes and subthemes on specific societal issues.

text.text: We used this flexible approach as a deductive analysis, making it suitable for our RQ 2, and qualitatively examined the collected research for common themes.

Following Braun and Clarke's (2006) six-phase approach, we began by (1) getting to know the data and immersing ourselves in it through repeated reading and transcription to build a solid understanding.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Braun and Clarke's (2006)</ref> six-phase approach, we began by (1) getting to know the data and immersing ourselves in it through repeated reading and transcription to build a solid understanding.

text.text: (2) Next, we generated initial codes, systematically identifying interesting features of the data and pulling them together to form potential themes.
(3) With a list of codes in hand, we identified themes by looking for broader patterns of meaning and considering how they fit within the set of included studies.

(4) In the review phase, we refined these candidate themes to ensure they accurately captured the included studies, checking how well they worked with both the included studies and the research field.
(5) We then defined and named our themes, giving each clear, distinct definitions that summarize its core ideas.

(6) Finally, we connected our narrative with the themes, creating a cohesive account of our findings, supported by key characteristics of the included studies that highlighted the essence of our themes.
By staying aware of our own presence in the analysis, we aimed to ensure that our conclusions were well-anchored in the set of included studies.
We approached the thematic analysis systematically, making our theoretical perspectives clear to enhance the study's transparency.
By following Braun and Clarke's (2006) approach, we qualitatively explored the complex set of included studies to address RQ 2 on common themes within the literature.
text.formatted: By following <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Braun and Clarke's (2006)</ref> approach, we qualitatively explored the complex set of included studies to address RQ 2 on common themes within the literature.

text.text: Our results are based on 68 articles identified from the 31 most-cited Educational Psychology journals.
First, we address RQ 1 by presenting descriptive results from our systematic literature review.
Second, we present the results of our thematic analysis in response to RQ 2.
As mentioned earlier, we address research gaps and future research (preregistered as RQ 3) in the Discussion.

To examine the extent of LGBTQ+ representation in the field of Educational Psychology, we draw on the counts and relative frequencies of LGBTQ+ themed articles per journal in Table 1, as well as the publication, sample, and design characteristics of the 68 included articles, illustrated in Table S3 in the online supplemental material.

text.text: Of the 31 most-cited journals, 14 published no LGBTQ+ themed articles.
This finding, that about half of the included journals did not publish any LGBTQ+ themed articles, is in line with our hypotheses and prior research (see M. H. Jones et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This finding, that about half of the included journals did not publish any LGBTQ+ themed articles, is in line with our hypotheses and prior research (see M. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Jones et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For example, we found no publications in two journals at the top of the ranking, Contemporary Educational Psychology and Learning and Instruction, despite both journals mentioning diversity and inclusivity in their aims and scope.
Of the 31 journals, 10 published one or two LGBTQ+ themed articles, with varying percentages.
For example, Educational Psychology Review published its first volume in 1989 and, as of December 2023, has published 714 articles, 2 (0.28%) of which address LGBTQ+ issues (see Table 1).
text.formatted: For example, Educational Psychology Review published its first volume in 1989 and, as of December 2023, has published 714 articles, 2 (0.28%) of which address LGBTQ+ issues (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The remaining 7 journals published more than two LGBTQ+ themed articles.
As the most prominent example, School Psychology Review published 25 articles on LGBTQ+ issues, amounting to 1.50% of the total 1,668 articles ever published in this journal.
The only other journal with more than 1% of its studies including LGBTQ+ topics was School Mental Health, with 5 articles (1.19%).
Just below this percentage were the journals School Psychology (0.84%), Journal of Literacy Research (0.83%), and Social Psychology of Education (0.55%).
Taken together, only 0.16% of all articles published in the 31 most-cited Educational Psychology journals include LGBTQ+ issues.

text.text: About 45 years ago, this marked the beginning of research on LGBTQ+ issues in today's most impactful Educational Psychology journals.

Another special issue of this journal was published in 2008, featuring four articles.
In summary, Figure 2 indicates an initially small extent of LGBTQ+ representation over the past century, with a growing trend in article publications in recent decades.

The 68 articles vary considerably in publication, sample, and design characteristics, but we observed several trends (see Table S3 online).
text.formatted: The 68 articles vary considerably in publication, sample, and design characteristics, but we observed several trends (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> online).

text.text: Regarding publication type, the 68 articles comprise 48 original research articles (70.59%), 13 literature reviews (19.12%; including narrative reviews, scoping reviews, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses), three editorials (4.41%), and opinion papers and commentaries.
No book reviews or article corrections were identified (see Table S3 online).
text.formatted: No book reviews or article corrections were identified (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> online).

text.text: Hence, the majority of published articles reported original research and literature reviews.
Regarding the design, both quantitative (n = 32; 47.06%) and qualitative (n = 30; 44.12%) methods were employed.
Five articles (7.35%) used a mixed-methods approach.
In total, 36 articles (52.94%) used a cross-sectional design, and most of these were based on selfreports or surveys (see Table S3 online).
text.formatted: In total, 36 articles (52.94%) used a cross-sectional design, and most of these were based on selfreports or surveys (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> online).

text.text: Another common design was reviews of major findings, with nine articles (13.24%) published as literature reviews, editorials, or opinion papers.
Other study designs included exploratory or observational designs.
None of the included studies were preregistered, and only 2 (3.85%) shared their data, analytical code, and materials and were published open access.
Naturally, these were somewhat recent articles, since the Open Science movement and related research standards are only some 10-15 years old (Bauer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Naturally, these were somewhat recent articles, since the Open Science movement and related research standards are only some 10-15 years old <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bauer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As for the country of origin, the majority of the articles (n = 43; 82,69%) were written by researchers from the U.S., followed by three articles (5.77%) from Italy and two (3.85%) from the U.K. There was one publication from each of Australia, Canada, Germany, and Spain (see Table S3 online).
text.formatted: As for the country of origin, the majority of the articles (n = 43; 82,69%) were written by researchers from the U.S., followed by three articles (5.77%) from Italy and two (3.85%) from the U.K. There was one publication from each of Australia, Canada, Germany, and Spain (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> online).

text.text: Thus, there seems to be a focus on cross-sectional designs and literature reviews from the U.S., while longitudinal studies and publications from diverse countries seem missing.
Regarding the sample characteristics of the 48 original research articles reporting sexual orientation and gender identity, 31 articles included samples comprising both non-LGBTQ+ and LGBTQ+ people.
Thus, in most studies, LGBTQ+ participants were compared with non-LGBTQ+ samples.
Twelve articles reported only participants' sexual identities, not gender identities.

Six (12.5%) drew on samples exclusively comprised of LGBTQ+ people (Fine et al., 2021; Horton, 2023; Lo et al., 2022; Mackie et al., 2021; Morris & Lent, 2019; Ollen et al., 2017; Peterson & Rischar, 2000).

text.text: The included articles reported various sample characteristics related to race, ethnicity, family, and socioeconomic status (see Table S3 online), highlighting the potential for investigating research questions on intersectionality.

text.text: The included studies varied considerably in how they assessed and reported sexual orientations and gender identities.

A total of 45 articles reporting gender identities of their samples used categories such as girl or boy or female or male to define either the sex or gender of participants, excluding agender and non-binary people.
Furthermore, none of the articles used the exact same selection of terms to report the sexual orientations of participants, which complicates comparing results between studies.
Table 2 illustrates the frequency of terms used to describe sexual orientation.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> illustrates the frequency of terms used to describe sexual orientation.

text.text: In total, the term bisexual was used most often across all articles, specifically in 23 (74.19%) of the 31 samples where sexual orientation was reported.
Next, the terms gay and lesbian were used in 19 (61.29%) and 18 (58.06%) publications, respectively.
Additionally, researchers used several versions of the LGBTQ+ acronym.
Terms seldomly reported to describe participants included pan-, demi-, and asexual.
Three articles (9.68%) did not concretely describe the sexual orientation of their sample, and one article (3.23%) asked participants an open-ended question about their sexual orientation.
Another relevant finding concerned the educational stakeholder the studies focused on.
These could be school students, educators, school personnel, or youth in general.
Table 3 shows the frequencies of these educational stakeholders across seven categories that Hattie (2009) used in his seminal second-order meta-analysis of factors of educational success.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> shows the frequencies of these educational stakeholders across seven categories that <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Hattie (2009)</ref> used in his seminal second-order meta-analysis of factors of educational success.

text.text: In the included studies, LGBTQ+ themed research most often drew on School Students (e.g., elementary, middle, and high school), with high school students in Grades 9 to 12 most represented.
Three articles drew on Caregivers and Other Adults (also including the general public; see Silva et al., 2022), and another three on Educators.
