What are the Common Themes in LGBTQ+ Centered Research in the Most-cited Journals of Educational Psychology?
To address RQ 2, we considered all data extracted in a thematic analysis.
Consistent with recommendations for thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), we included variables, research questions, and results of the 68 included articles.
text.formatted: Consistent with recommendations for thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Braun & Clarke, 2006)</ref>, we included variables, research questions, and results of the 68 included articles.

text.text: Combining this information, we extracted seven themes (ordered by frequency, displayed in parentheses): 1.
Homophobic bullying and victimization (n = 18) 2.
Protective factors for LGBTQ+ people (n = 15) 3.
LGBTQ+ advocacy in schools (n = 9) 4.
LGBTQ+ curricula in schools (n = 8) 5.
Youth-related risks (n = 7) 6.
Intersectionality of multiple minority identities (n = 6) 7.
Mental health vulnerabilities (n = 5) See the extended description of the seven themes with examples in Table S4.
text.formatted: Mental health vulnerabilities (n = 5) See the extended description of the seven themes with examples in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S4</ref>.

text.text: Examining the frequency of these seven themes shows that LGBTQ+ themed research focuses more on deficitoriented themes (n = 37; i.e., homophobic bullying and victimization, youth-related risks, intersectionalities of multiple minority identities, mental health vulnerabilities) than strengthoriented ones (n = 31; i.e., protective factors of LGBTQ+ people, LGBTQ+ advocacy, LGBTQ+ curricula in schools).
This preregistered systematic literature review provides a comprehensive overview of LGBTQ+ representation in Educational Psychology.

In response to RQ 1, our findings from the 68 retrieved articles confirmed our expectations that LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology is limited, accounting for only 0.16% of all published research in the 31 most-cited journals in the field available in ERIC.
However, we also observed an increase in LGBTQ+ centered research in the field.
Addressing RQ 2, we identified seven common themes in the included literature.

Although we expected a strong focus on deficit-oriented topics, such as Homophobic Bullying and Victimization, Youth-Related Risks, Intersectionality of Multiple Minority Identities, and Mental Health Vulnerabilities, we also found considerable attention to strength-oriented themes, including Protective Factors for LGBTQ+ people, LGBTQ+ Advocacy in Schools, and LGBTQ+ Curricula in Schools.

After first discussing RQ 1 and RQ2, we derive research gaps from the current literature to address the preregistered RQ 3 and shed light on the significance of LGBTQ+ inclusion in Educational Psychology.
LGBTQ+ centered research is scarce in Educational Psychology journals.
We found zero search results in 14 of the 31 included journals, similar to the findings of Jones et al.'s (2018) literature review.
text.formatted: We found zero search results in 14 of the 31 included journals, similar to the findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Jones et al.'s (2018)</ref> literature review.

text.text: If journals did publish LGBTQ+ centered research, most listed only one or two articles (see Table 1).
text.formatted: If journals did publish LGBTQ+ centered research, most listed only one or two articles (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: With only 0.16% of all published articles in these journals addressing LGBTQ+ issues, compared with more than 20% of students identifying as LGBTQ+ and thus facing additional challenges (Gallup, 2022; Kosciw et al., 2022), this figure is rather small.
text.formatted: With only 0.16% of all published articles in these journals addressing LGBTQ+ issues, compared with more than 20% of students identifying as LGBTQ+ and thus facing additional challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Gallup, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Kosciw et al., 2022)</ref>, this figure is rather small.

text.text: There are several reasons the extent of LGBTQ+ representation in Educational Psychology journals is so low.

The first article published in these journals in 1981-poignantly on the precarious situation of school psychologists considering disclosing their LGBTQ+ identity (Alpert et al., 1981)-reflects the difficult situation of LGBTQ+ people in large parts of the 20 th century.
text.formatted: The first article published in these journals in 1981-poignantly on the precarious situation of school psychologists considering disclosing their LGBTQ+ identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Alpert et al., 1981</ref>)-reflects the difficult situation of LGBTQ+ people in large parts of the 20 th century.

text.text: Additionally, many articles do not report on sexual or gender minorities in their samples.
When these characteristics are reported, the terms used to describe sexual orientation, for example, are inconsistent (see Table 2).
text.formatted: When these characteristics are reported, the terms used to describe sexual orientation, for example, are inconsistent (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: In part, a clear distinction between sex and gender is lacking, as terms are conflated.
These findings suggest a need for more detailed reporting of gender and sexual orientation.
However, because the LGBTQ+ acronym is everchanging, it is difficult to determine which terms are best to describe samples.
Thus, we recommend comprehensive reporting of gender diversity and sexual orientation, informed by widely accepted guidelines (e.g., American Psychological Association, 2023; Lindqvist et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Thus, we recommend comprehensive reporting of gender diversity and sexual orientation, informed by widely accepted guidelines (e.g., American Psychological Association, 2023; <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Lindqvist et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While including people of diverse genders and sexual orientations does not yet render a research article LGBTQ+ centered, it promotes representation and visibility.
However, LGBTQ+ samples can be hard to come by.
Therefore, research on LGBTQ+ people often relies on snowball sampling.
This, in turn, makes publication in one of the highestranked journals less likely because representative data for survey studies or randomized controlled trials with LGBTQ+ people are scarce.

Also, not all LGBTQ+ people will choose to disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity just for taking part in an interview or survey study (Macapagal et al., 2017), further skewing the sample characteristics.
text.formatted: Also, not all LGBTQ+ people will choose to disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity just for taking part in an interview or survey study <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Macapagal et al., 2017)</ref>, further skewing the sample characteristics.

text.text: Consequently, many articles only urge future research to investigate LGBTQ+ issues and people but do not report findings on these topics or samples themselves.
It is further debated whether LGBTQ+ topics are stigmatized and whether LGBTQ+ researchers may be labeled as activists with an agenda if they study their own community (Harrison & Michelson, 2022).
text.formatted: It is further debated whether LGBTQ+ topics are stigmatized and whether LGBTQ+ researchers may be labeled as activists with an agenda if they study their own community <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Harrison & Michelson, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, LGBTQ+ researchers and their work may face additional hurdles to be taken seriously.
This stigmatization might also explain the scarcity of professorships in educational LGBTQ+ research.

Additionally, changes in national policy on LGBTQ+ or general diversity research, as currently seen in the US, are likely to severely affect the representation of LGBTQ+ topics in top-ranking Educational Psychology journals.
All these factors, and several more, are diminishing LGBTQ+ representation not only in Educational Psychology.
We are, however, optimistic that LGBTQ+ themed publications will increase in the future.
First, research on other minorities in other fields shows a rise in attention similar to LGBTQ+ research, and there is no indication of a decline in research on any of these minorities.

As with LGBTQ+ centered research, Jing et al. (2020) found a steep increase in research on international students after 2000, with most studies originating in the US or the UK. Mongeon et al. (2021) reported a similar publication trajectory in Library and Information Science, with a surge after 2000 on Black People, Indigenous People, and People of Color, as did Lazić (2024) for gifted students in Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics education.
text.formatted: As with LGBTQ+ centered research, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Jing et al. (2020)</ref> found a steep increase in research on international students after 2000, with most studies originating in the US or the UK. <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Mongeon et al. (2021)</ref> reported a similar publication trajectory in Library and Information Science, with a surge after 2000 on Black People, Indigenous People, and People of Color, as did Lazić (2024) for gifted students in Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics education.

text.text: Thus, the current scarcity, and more broadly the surge in interest in LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology mirrors research on other minority groups and other fields.

This pattern might reflect research fields first working with their general core samples (e.g., cisgender, heterosexual, ethnic majority students) before expanding their efforts to marginalized groups (e.g., LGBTQ+ and other minorities).
Second, we see an increase in LGBTQ+ themed publications after 2000.
This increase may be attributed to considerable legal progress in most Western societies (see, e.g., Ayoub, 2016, for a cross-European perspective).

Further, the rise in internet usage might have led to both a general increase in publications (see Bornmann et al., 2021) through the digitalization of publication processes and to social media usage around the turn of the century.
text.formatted: Further, the rise in internet usage might have led to both a general increase in publications (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bornmann et al., 2021)</ref> through the digitalization of publication processes and to social media usage around the turn of the century.

text.text: In particular, social media has significantly contributed to LGBTQ+ inclusivity and representation by providing a safe space for communication, learning, and self-education on LGBTQ+ issues (Lucero, 2017).
text.formatted: In particular, social media has significantly contributed to LGBTQ+ inclusivity and representation by providing a safe space for communication, learning, and self-education on LGBTQ+ issues <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Lucero, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, social media content can shape the discourse of young people in schools, including LGBTQ+ issues (D. Boyd, 2020).
text.formatted: Importantly, social media content can shape the discourse of young people in schools, including LGBTQ+ issues (D. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Boyd, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This general increase in LGBTQ+ visibility may also lead to increased publication figures on the topic.
Third, generational change might be a driver of increased LGBTQ+ representation in research.

Not only do we see more study participants identifying as LGBTQ+ across generations (Gallup, 2022; Ipsos, 2023), but an increasing number of researchers and journal editors also identify as LGBTQ+ or are allies, experience greater support in their work environments (Veldhuis, 2022), and are more likely to acknowledge the added value LGBTQ+ research can bring to the field.
text.formatted: Not only do we see more study participants identifying as LGBTQ+ across generations <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Gallup, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ipsos, 2023)</ref>, but an increasing number of researchers and journal editors also identify as LGBTQ+ or are allies, experience greater support in their work environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">(Veldhuis, 2022)</ref>, and are more likely to acknowledge the added value LGBTQ+ research can bring to the field.

text.text: Fourth, there could be a reciprocal relationship between the increasing visibility of LGBTQ+ research in Educational Psychology journals, supported by more inclusive editorial policies, and the likelihood of successful publication and long-term field growth.

Fifth, research continues to reveal disparities in safety, belonging, and academic outcomes for LGBTQ+ students, as well as methodological research gaps. Leung et al. (2022), for example, shows that LGBTQ-inclusive climates reduce depression, dropout, and social isolation, emphasizing the ongoing need for school-based psychological studies that address these risks through inclusive pedagogies and interventions.
text.formatted: Fifth, research continues to reveal disparities in safety, belonging, and academic outcomes for LGBTQ+ students, as well as methodological research gaps. <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Leung et al. (2022)</ref>, for example, shows that LGBTQ-inclusive climates reduce depression, dropout, and social isolation, emphasizing the ongoing need for school-based psychological studies that address these risks through inclusive pedagogies and interventions.

text.text: This further raises practitioners' demand for applied psychological research to close the practice-research divide (Abreu et al., 2022; Davies et al., 2025; Leung et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This further raises practitioners' demand for applied psychological research to close the practice-research divide <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abreu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Davies et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Leung et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Now, what can researchers do to increase their chances of publishing LGBTQ+ centered research in most-cited Educational Psychology journals?
Twice, a group of articles was published in special issues of the journal School Psychology Review.
These special issues were the drivers of the first peak in publications in 2000 and the peak in 2008 (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: These special issues were the drivers of the first peak in publications in 2000 and the peak in 2008 (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Beyond banding together for special issues, much remains to be done.

Thus, we discuss pertinent research gaps in the field, the importance of inclusive samples and the inclusion of a wide range of educational stakeholders, and make recommendations for rigorous research methods to build a robust evidence base.
We identified several pressing gaps in LGBTQ+ centered research in most-cited Educational Psychology journals, addressing our preregistered RQ 3.
Table 4 presents these gaps in an Evidence Gap Map that crosses the seven research themes we identified in RQ 2 and Hattie's (2009) taxonomy of educational settings.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref> presents these gaps in an Evidence Gap Map that crosses the seven research themes we identified in RQ 2 and <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Hattie's (2009)</ref> taxonomy of educational settings.

text.text: The most researched themes are Homophobic Bullying and Victimization and Protective Factors for LGBTQ+ People.
In particular, a common topic of interest is the relationship between homophobic victimization and mental health vulnerabilities (e.g., Price et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In particular, a common topic of interest is the relationship between homophobic victimization and mental health vulnerabilities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Price et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Much less research was published on LGBTQ+ Advocacy in Schools, Youth-Related Risks, LGBTQ+ Curricula in Schools, Intersectionality of Multiple Minority Identities, and Mental Health Vulnerabilities (e.g., Edwards, 2021).
text.formatted: Much less research was published on LGBTQ+ Advocacy in Schools, Youth-Related Risks, LGBTQ+ Curricula in Schools, Intersectionality of Multiple Minority Identities, and Mental Health Vulnerabilities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Edwards, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Addressing our hypothesis that there would be more deficit-oriented than strength-oriented research on LGBTQ+ issues, 37 articles examined a deficit-oriented theme while 31 investigated a strength-oriented one.

Therefore, research on deficit-oriented themes indeed outweighs research on strength-oriented themes in descriptive terms, but a descriptive temporal trend suggests an increase in strength-oriented themes in recent years.

As for Hattie's (2009) taxonomy of educational settings, we find most research on Students and Schools, whereas Classrooms, Teachers, Home environments, Curricula, and Learning situations were much less researched (see Table 4).
text.formatted: As for Hattie's (2009) taxonomy of educational settings, we find most research on Students and Schools, whereas Classrooms, Teachers, Home environments, Curricula, and Learning situations were much less researched (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: As a result, we were able to identify several areas for research that could be prominently published in the future.

Investigating the mental health vulnerabilities and intersectionality of multiple minority identities among teachers, other school personnel, and in the home environment is clearly lacking (see Table 4).
text.formatted: Investigating the mental health vulnerabilities and intersectionality of multiple minority identities among teachers, other school personnel, and in the home environment is clearly lacking (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: None of the most-cited journals' articles shed light on key issues in LGBTQ+ teacher mental health.

Additionally, research in the classroom should address not only deficit-oriented issues (e.g., homophobic bullying and victimization) but also strength-oriented issues, such as protective factors for LGBTQ+ people and LGBTQ+ advocacy on the classroom level.
A closer review of the included studies suggested that many more articles reported samples composed of LGBTQ+ students than of educators, other school personnel, or caregivers (see Table 3).
text.formatted: A closer review of the included studies suggested that many more articles reported samples composed of LGBTQ+ students than of educators, other school personnel, or caregivers (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Notably, none of these samples came from special education schools, indicating another research gap.
Most samples consisted of American middle and high school students-the age when sexuality becomes more central to one's identity (Erikson, 1968 (Erikson, , 2013)).
text.formatted: Most samples consisted of American middle and high school students-the age when sexuality becomes more central to one's identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Erikson, 1968</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Erikson, , 2013))</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, only a small body of research focused on tertiary educational settings, such as universities (e.g., Ollen et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Similarly, only a small body of research focused on tertiary educational settings, such as universities (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Ollen et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: While research in higher education is generally less frequent in the most-cited journals, research on and with LGBTQ+ populations in higher education must be expanded to ensure LGBTQ+ inclusivity university teaching and learning (see Wimberly, 2015, Chapter 8).
text.formatted: While research in higher education is generally less frequent in the most-cited journals, research on and with LGBTQ+ populations in higher education must be expanded to ensure LGBTQ+ inclusivity university teaching and learning (see <ref type="bibr">Wimberly, 2015, Chapter 8)</ref>.

text.text: Another gap in LGBTQ+ representation in Educational Psychology concerns curricula.
Several articles examined how LGBTQ+ inclusive literature can help counteract normative thinking in students (e.g., Blackburn & Schey, 2018).
text.formatted: Several articles examined how LGBTQ+ inclusive literature can help counteract normative thinking in students (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Blackburn & Schey, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, this research focused on humanities courses, and none of the articles we identified evaluated the impact of LGBTQ+inclusive curricula in other subjects, such as biology, on LGBTQ+-inclusive sex education (Gegenfurtner & Gebhardt, 2017).
text.formatted: However, this research focused on humanities courses, and none of the articles we identified evaluated the impact of LGBTQ+inclusive curricula in other subjects, such as biology, on LGBTQ+-inclusive sex education <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Gegenfurtner & Gebhardt, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This research might, however, be published not in Educational Psychology journals but in subject-specific didactics.
Still, we find no mention of resources to educate school personnel on the importance of LGBTQ+ inclusion in curricula.
Resources should be more widespread, comprehensive, and accessible for all types of institutions.
Further skewing the existing literature, all included studies were conducted with samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) countries (Henrich et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Further skewing the existing literature, all included studies were conducted with samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Henrich et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Non-Western samples were entirely absent.

Differences in school systems and cultures matter for many aspects of Educational Psychology, such as interpersonal relationships (Emslander et al., 2025), but contrasts between countries may be even starker for LGBTQ+ issues.
text.formatted: Differences in school systems and cultures matter for many aspects of Educational Psychology, such as interpersonal relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Emslander et al., 2025)</ref>, but contrasts between countries may be even starker for LGBTQ+ issues.

text.text: Jurisdictions in several countries still criminalize LGBTQ+ people (Human Dignity Trust, n.d.), making research on them dangerous and potentially illegal.

The educational experiences of LGBTQ+ people in countries and cultures that do not recognize LGBTQ+ identities may be entirely different, yet this is not represented in the reviewed scientific literature.

Thus, the findings from the most-cited Educational Psychology journals on LGBTQ+ issues are very limited in their generalizability, since they cannot represent LGBTQ+ people globally and need to be expanded to include more diverse, non-WEIRD samples from around the world.
Similarly, not all people under the LGBTQ+ umbrella are equally represented in the most-cited journals.
We identified an overall lack of inclusion of minority gender identities.
There is a significant dearth of studies focusing on transphobic bullying and the broader issues faced by transgender and gender-nonconforming people in educational settings.
However, some findings highlight pervasive transphobic attitudes, transhysteria, or microaggressions (Horton, 2023; Mackie et al., 2021; Shevlin & Gill, 2020).
text.formatted: However, some findings highlight pervasive transphobic attitudes, transhysteria, or microaggressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Horton, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Mackie et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Shevlin & Gill, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should examine protective factors and actionable guidance for students, teachers, and other school personnel who identify as gender minorities.
In a similar vein, the research disregards the nuances of different sexual orientations.

There are differences between the experiences of a gay or lesbian adolescent with more visible role models, representation in the media or culture, and growing acceptance, compared with those of a bisexual adolescent.

This lack of representation and exclusion from both heterosexual and gay or lesbian in-groups can lead to health problems (Elia, 2014) and is linked to school avoidance and substance abuse (Darwich et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This lack of representation and exclusion from both heterosexual and gay or lesbian in-groups can lead to health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Elia, 2014)</ref> and is linked to school avoidance and substance abuse <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Darwich et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In society, sexual and gender identities are often treated as a dichotomy, which erases both people whose sexual orientation is fluid or who identify outside of monosexual identities and the gender binary.
This is underscored by a general scarcity of research on bisexuality (Elia, 2014).
text.formatted: This is underscored by a general scarcity of research on bisexuality <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Elia, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, future research should also focus on people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity beyond such dichotomies, since they might be especially vulnerable (Stewart, 2021).
text.formatted: Thus, future research should also focus on people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity beyond such dichotomies, since they might be especially vulnerable <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Stewart, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, we identified that research on several subgroups within the LGBTQ+ umbrella is entirely missing, such as asexual or aromantic people.
Youth grow up surrounded by an inherent expectation to experience sexual and romantic attraction (Zamani-Gallaher et al., 2020, Chapter 6).
text.formatted: Youth grow up surrounded by an inherent expectation to experience sexual and romantic attraction <ref type="bibr">(Zamani-Gallaher et al., 2020, Chapter 6)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, such allosexual norms and compulsory sexuality are put forward from a young age, leading asexual and aromantic people to feel marginalized (Zamani-Gallaher et al., 2020, Chapter 6).
text.formatted: Thus, such allosexual norms and compulsory sexuality are put forward from a young age, leading asexual and aromantic people to feel marginalized <ref type="bibr">(Zamani-Gallaher et al., 2020, Chapter 6)</ref>.

text.text: Resulting isolation from peers can negatively affect well-being and academic achievement (e.g., Swearer et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Resulting isolation from peers can negatively affect well-being and academic achievement (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Swearer et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, none of the included articles investigated intersex populations.

In particular, intersex adolescents may experience puberty differently from peers whose sex characteristics fit normative medical ideas for female or male bodies, which may contribute to experiences of exclusion and bullying (T. Jones, 2016).
text.formatted: In particular, intersex adolescents may experience puberty differently from peers whose sex characteristics fit normative medical ideas for female or male bodies, which may contribute to experiences of exclusion and bullying (T. <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Jones, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a wide range of LGBTQ+ subgroups must be investigated in research to lay the groundwork for advocacy for all people under the LGBTQ+ umbrella in educational settings.
This is especially relevant for multiply minoritized people.
Future research must remain mindful of the differences among LGBTQ+ identities.
Overall, in research on various LGBTQ+ populations, sexual and gender identity should be viewed as fluid, especially when studying youth (Diamond, 2016 (Diamond, , 2020)).
text.formatted: Overall, in research on various LGBTQ+ populations, sexual and gender identity should be viewed as fluid, especially when studying youth <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Diamond, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Diamond, , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, novel ways to assess sexual and gender identity-such as including a certainty rating for sexual orientation in youth to allow for fluidity-need to be developed, validated, and used in research.
In addition to a broader variation of topics and samples, more diverse and robust methods should be used in LGBTQ+ centered research.
Findings from Table S3 (Supplemental Material) indicate that many empirical studies use cross-sectional rather than longitudinal or intervention research designs.
text.formatted: Findings from Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref> (Supplemental Material) indicate that many empirical studies use cross-sectional rather than longitudinal or intervention research designs.

text.text: However, the latter designs are especially important for examining temporal change and the efficacy of interventions, for example, anti-bullying or awareness programs.

Negative teacher attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people (see e.g., Galano et al., 2024), for example, can determine a teacher's willingness to intervene in a bullying situation, or, in turn, jeopardize the safety of an educational environment (e.g., Gegenfurtner et al., 2023; Hall & Rodgers, 2019).
text.formatted: Negative teacher attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people (see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Galano et al., 2024)</ref>, for example, can determine a teacher's willingness to intervene in a bullying situation, or, in turn, jeopardize the safety of an educational environment (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Gegenfurtner et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Hall & Rodgers, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, longitudinal and intervention research is needed to specifically examine the impact of bullying interventions on teacher attitudes and, more generally, on support programs for LGBTQ+ people in educational settings.

While the current landscape of LGBTQ+ research in most-cited Educational Psychology journals shows early steps toward Open Science, with two of 68 articles already adhering to key standards such as data sharing and open access, there remains substantial potential for growth.
It is important to note that many studies were conducted before Open Science strategies were widely established or formalized.

Moving forward, researchers should, whenever possible, (1) preregister their studies to safeguard against p-hacking and post hoc hypothesis changes, (2) openly share their data, code, and materials to invite colleagues to trace and replicate their findings and foster collaboration, and (3) publish their articles open access (resources permitting) to enable wide distribution and accessibility of their work.
Adopting Open Science standards (Bauer et al., 2026) will further strengthen the transparency and reproducibility of evidence in LGBTQ+ research.
text.formatted: Adopting Open Science standards <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bauer et al., 2026)</ref> will further strengthen the transparency and reproducibility of evidence in LGBTQ+ research.

text.text: While we conducted our study in accordance with current guidelines for systematic reviews (Page et al., 2021), scientometric research (Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012), and qualitative thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), our methods and the article's scope have inherent constraints on generality.
text.formatted: While we conducted our study in accordance with current guidelines for systematic reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Page et al., 2021)</ref>, scientometric research <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Leydesdorff & Milojević, 2012)</ref>, and qualitative thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Braun & Clarke, 2006)</ref>, our methods and the article's scope have inherent constraints on generality.

text.text: As in every systematic review, we are likely to encounter publication bias (McShane et al., 2016).
text.formatted: As in every systematic review, we are likely to encounter publication bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(McShane et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: That is, studies with statistically non-significant results are less likely to be published and, thus, less likely to be included in our review of published articles (Ferguson & Heene, 2012).
text.formatted: That is, studies with statistically non-significant results are less likely to be published and, thus, less likely to be included in our review of published articles <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Ferguson & Heene, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This shifts the evidence base toward significant results through selective publication and may thus affect the representation of specific research topics.
Furthermore, our database is limited to the articles available through and indexed and, thus, findable in ERIC through EBSCOhost at the time of search.
The scientometric research method has several limitations.

First, longitudinal analysis is subject to compositional shifts within journals: the evolving scope and editorial focus of academic journals, along with changes in journal rankings over time, may influence publication patterns independently of research trends.
Second, establishing a reliable demographic baseline for LGBTQ+ representation remains a significant challenge.

Thus, it is difficult to determine a 'reasonable expectation' for the frequency of LGBTQ+ focused research based solely on general population percentages, research on other minorities, or baseline figures of published articles.

Furthermore, many articles in Educational Psychology address broad psychological phenomena that are not inherently targeted toward specific identity groups, making a direct proportional comparison between population demographics and research output conceptually complex.
Qualitative thematic analyses are, of course, subjective and may yield different results when conducted by different researchers.
We have tried to counteract this by working closely together as an author team and discussing the qualitative results until consensus was reached.
We also openly share our materials in the online supplement to make our research process as transparent as possible.
The Evidence Gap Map (Table 4) presents themes identified in research across educational settings.
text.formatted: The Evidence Gap Map (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>) presents themes identified in research across educational settings.

text.text: However, not every theme (e.g., homophobic bullying) can be directly mapped onto Hattie's (2009) taxonomy of educational settings used (e.g., curricula).
text.formatted: However, not every theme (e.g., homophobic bullying) can be directly mapped onto <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Hattie's (2009)</ref> taxonomy of educational settings used (e.g., curricula).

text.text: Therefore, we only discussed meaningful gaps in the literature.

The scope of our systematic review was the 41,992 published journal articles available in ERIC from the two upper quartiles of Educational Psychology, based on their Journal Impact Factor (Clarivate, 2024) as of December 2023.
While we focused on LGBTQ+ representation in Educational Psychology, perhaps pertinent issues are being researched in other fields, such as clinical psychology, counseling psychology, or education.
Thus, future replications of this review may attend to LGBTQ+ representation in other fields of psychology and beyond.
In this preregistered systematic scientometric review, we summarized more than 100 years of LGBTQ+ representation in the most-cited Educational Psychology journals.

Based on 68 LGBTQ+ centered articles among the 41,992 articles available in ERIC published in the 31 Q1 and Q2 journals in the field, we identified the extent and trends of LGBTQ+ centered research (RQ 1), common themes (RQ 2), and research gaps.
First, we confirmed our expectations that LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology is small.
With a first publication in 1981, it accounts for only 0.16% of the sample.
However, research activity in LGBTQ+ centered Educational Psychology appears to be increasing.
If this trend continues, the number of publications in high-ranking journals may someday match the importance of supporting sexual and gender minorities in educational settings.
Notably, our findings suggest that special issues can help publish LGBTQ+ centered research in these journals.

Second, we found more deficit-oriented themes, such as Homophobic Bullying and Victimization and Youth-Related Risks, but strength-oriented themes also gained attention, such as Protective Factors for LGBTQ+ people and LGBTQ+ Advocacy in Schools.
Third, we provided suggestions for future research on topics, samples, and methods.
Future scientometric analyses should expand to neighboring disciplines to assess and help increase LGBTQ+ representation.
